meta.subtitle: An Atlas of Death, Folklore, Landscape, Decay, Memory and the Unseen
meta.editorial_note: All visible text is in English. Russian terms are given in simplified transliteration with a gloss. plates.title: THE THRESHOLD
plates.subtitle: The room, the moment, and the border that is not drawn
plates.dek: The ethnography of death in Russia is rarely an account of dying. It is an account of what the living do in the room afterwards — and of how quickly that room becomes a border.
plates.marginal: The mirror and the water are documented in the sources read for this edition. The open window is documented for Eastern Slavic rites in general. The stopped clock is repeated in the literature, but none of those sources records it.
plates.tradition: Orthodox Christian practice; local folk custom

sections.heading: A room with the window open
paras: In the accounts collected by ethnographers in Russian villages from the middle of the nineteenth century onward, death is registered less as an event than as a series of adjustments to a house. Mirrors are covered. Water standing in the house is thrown out or covered. The body is washed and laid on a bench, feet toward the door, men to the right of the entrance and women to the left; the table is a recent habit, chiefly Belarusian, and some Russian Old Believers lay the dead with the feet toward the icons (Zelenin 1991, pp. 347–348). At the moment of death the stove flues or a small window are opened and a piece of linen or a towel is hung out of the window; Zelenin reports three popular readings: the soul wipes itself with it, wipes its tears, or rests on it (p. 346). A stopped clock is often named, but no source read for this edition records it, so it is not asserted.

These are the practices most often repeated in the literature, and they are the ones most often flattened into a single ‘Russian custom’. The sources do not support that flattening. They record variants; they record disagreement between villages a day’s walk apart; and they record the informant’s own uncertainty about why a thing was done.

Barsov’s first volume (1872), from the Olonets North, describes the same room with differences. The dead person is laid on straw spread on the bench in the front corner, head toward the icons, with copper coins on the eyes; the house is kept quiet and is either not swept or swept toward the dead, so that others do not die (p. 303). Zelenin’s account above has the feet toward the door, so the two sources disagree on orientation and neither makes a rule. Barsov also says that a piece of linen was hung outside the window, or toward the outer front corner, for forty days after a death, and calls the custom general in Novgorod province; in Korela, when the priest was seen approaching, the window frame was taken out and a patterned towel hung there, because the dead were believed to enter a house through the window, not the door (p. 308). At Chimkinichi a pupil of his saw the frame taken out so that the dead could be carried out through the window, though the usual way out was by the door and the stairs (p. 305).

sections.heading: The soul as breath, and as a guest
paras: Russian folk belief, as described by Linda Ivanits and by D. K. Zelenin before her, treats the soul (*dusha*) as a substance closely bound to breath and to the body’s warmth, and simultaneously as a person-like visitor who must be housed, fed and escorted. The same informants use both descriptions in a single account.

The consequence is a threshold that is both physical and social. The dead remain members of the household for a defined period, are addressed in the second person, and are given food and a place at the table. The border is maintained by small prohibitions rather than by a wall.

sections.heading: Premonitions, and the problem of the motif
paras: A dog howling at night, a bird striking the window, a beam groaning in the wall, a double shadow: the folkloric record is full of signs read retrospectively as announcements of a death. Published collections treat them as motifs, not as statistics. No source used here establishes how widely any single sign was believed, and retrospective reading makes such reports structurally unreliable.

sections.heading: Three claims and what was checked
items: That the mirror was covered to prevent the soul from being trapped. The practice is widely reported; the explanation is supplied by later writers and varies.

That a body was carried out feet first. Zelenin reports it for northern Russians: the coffin was carried out open, feet first, so that the dead could not see the way back, and struck three times on the threshold of the house; in Olonets province it went out through the window (citing Barsov, vol. 1, p. 306), elsewhere through the back door or the cattle shed, and a woman with a bath-broom swept behind the procession (1991, pp. 348–349). Its age and wider distribution remain unverified.

That the forty-day period is pre-Christian in origin. The scheme is documented in Orthodox liturgical handbooks; the claim that it continues an older pagan calendar is an interpretation, and a contested one.

sections.heading: Forty days in one district, and a dissenting encyclopedia
paras: One regional description gives the threshold a length. In Belozersk district, Vologda oblast, informants born between 1898 and 1935 told I. I. Razova that mirrors are covered for forty days; that coins are put on the window of the room where the body lies, then thrown into the grave to ‘buy’ the burial place; and that the door is not bolted for the whole forty days, because the dead are thought to come back until the fortieth day, sometimes as a bird at the window. A laundry beater across the doorway or rowan at the threshold keeps him out. The body lies three days on a bench. Set beside the opened window of the first section, this is the opposite gesture: one practice lets the soul out, the other leaves the way in unbarred and then guards it. Whether these belong to one logic is the atlas’s question, not the informants’. The Great Russian Encyclopedia’s entry on East Slavic funerary rites, read only in extract, takes the other side of the plate’s claim about variants: it calls the rite on the whole uniform and stable, with local differences on the surface. The atlas keeps both statements, and notes that the first is a single district’s account of the 20th century, while the second is a synthesis across a much larger area.

plates.title: THE BODY
plates.subtitle: Washing, dressing, carrying
plates.dek: Before it becomes a memory, the dead is an object that must be handled. The handling is the ritual.

sections.heading: Washing, and where the water goes
paras: Zelenin’s survey of East Slavic funeral rites puts the washing first: the body is washed in warm water and dressed in new clothes, and in many places this was once done while the dying person was still alive, because people believed one appears in the next world in the clothes in which one died. Since the moment of death is hard to catch, he suggests, washing the already dead became usual. A vessel of water stood beside the dying person for the soul to bathe in; some said they had seen the water stir. It stayed on the table or the windowsill for forty days, and some held that the soul drank from it (Zelenin 1991, pp. 345–346).

For Russians he lists what happened to everything used in the last washing: the vessel, the washcloth, the straw on which the person died, sometimes the boards. These were carried to the field or beyond the village edge, and the vessel was usually smashed. In spring they could be thrown into a river in flood; if the master of the house had died they were often buried in the yard ‘so that the domovoi should not die out’ (citing Zavoiko, p. 91). The place where they lay inspired dread. Water that happened to be standing in the house at the moment of death was not drunk but poured out. A pregnant woman must not wash the dead, or her child will die. Ukrainians, he adds, poured the water where neither people nor animals walk, between two outbuildings or under a maize drier; that is a comparison, not Russian evidence (p. 346).

Zelenin’s details come from the archive of the Russian Geographical Society and from regional collectors, cited by volume and number, and the book is a synthesis of Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian material. This edition read his passage; it did not see the archive files behind it. An earlier version of this section said the washers were commonly older women from outside the family and were paid in soap, towels or money. The passage read here says nothing of the kind, and the statement is withdrawn until a source is found.

Barsov gives a compact Olonets version of the same sequence. The dead person is usually washed with warm water on straw, opposite the chimney, from a clay vessel and rubbed twice with soap; in some places, Kondushi among them, a dead woman’s hair is cut and put in the coffin. The soap is then thrown into the river and the water poured out there, though sometimes both are kept: he says that sorcerers use the water to harm newly-weds, that a person made to drink it will waste away, and that the soap is used against fever (1872, p. 303). The sorcery beliefs are reported, not observed; the passage does not name an informant or say who did the washing.

sections.heading: Dress, and the ban on iron
paras: Many old people sewed their own death clothes in advance and put them on before major feasts and in violent thunderstorms; the clothes were mostly white. If they were sewn for someone already dead, the seams were made with the needle pointing away from the sewer and toward the dead, in places with the left hand, and an old shirt was torn off, not unbuttoned. No outer garment was put on the dead; its place was taken by a *savan*, which could be a white shirt closed like a sack, or a length of cloth wrapped round and bound with a long strip. Modern or smart clothes were not used. Instead of boots, bast shoes or soft cloth footwear (*kaligi*); if the dead were already in boots, the iron nails were pulled out (Zelenin 1991, pp. 346–347).

Cross and belt were strictly required, a copper cross, since silver was not allowed, sometimes a wooden one. A woman never wore an apron; a man always had a hat, laid beside the body if the priest objected. A girl who died unmarried was dressed as for a wedding, with a ring on the middle finger of the right hand, gifts distributed by her kin as at a wedding and a wedding loaf on the coffin lid; for her, and sometimes for a young man, a bachelor could be chosen as ‘groom’ to walk behind the coffin. Zelenin generalises these practices for the East Slavs; he does not date them or separate Russians from the others in every detail, so each belongs here to the region and group he names, where he names one.

Barsov (1872, p. 303) says that in some places the dying person was asked beforehand what he wished to wear. For the Petrozavodsk, Olonets and Povenets districts he lists white boots or shoes sewn with one waxed thread, a shirt with a belt and a bone comb, a white *balakhon* with a sash over it, and a length of linen as a cover; in many Kargopol parishes a shroud was put on over a plain shirt. A cross on a woollen thread was always added, and for an Old Believer a prayer rope as well. Clothes for the dead were sewn ‘inside out’, the needle pointing away from the sewer, which agrees with the seam rule above. His white boots or shoes differ from the bast shoes and soft footwear that Zelenin gives; the two describe different places and are not made to agree here.

sections.heading: The coffin and what went into it

meta.Material: Planks; surviving dugout examples in northern descriptions

paras: The Russian word *domovina* and the older *koloda* name a coffin once made from a single trunk, with a small window and the head end often rounded; Zelenin says that by his time coffins were made of boards, fastened with wooden pegs, not iron nails, in places with bast. Pious people used to make their own coffins in advance, which was taken as a sign of long life, and scattered grain in them and gave grain to beggars (1991, p. 348). Shavings from the boards and dry leaves of the bath-broom were the usual bedding; the pillow was cut from the cloth of the burial clothes or from hay and stitched on three sides.

Zelenin lists what was put in: bread, sometimes salt and butter, an egg at Easter, until recently a bottle of vodka for a man; copper coins tied in a kerchief at the belt, and coins in the grave. People read the coins differently: as payment for the burial place, as a way to keep the cattle from following the master (OR RGO, III, 1102), or, in the later reading, as a fare for crossing the fiery river or to pay off debts. For Belarusian forest areas he lists personal items, a pipe, a pouch, a child’s toy, a craftsman’s small tools, which he does not tie to Russians. The popular claim that the handmade coffin gave way to a bought one is not in this passage and is not supported by any source read for this plate.

sections.heading: Why the body is a difficult archive
items: The body leaves no object. What survives is the description of the objects that surrounded it, written down later, often by outsiders.
Ethnographers of the nineteenth century tended to record what they judged to be old. The date of a practice is therefore often the date of its recording, not of its origin.

sections.heading: Where the water goes, and what the soap keeps
paras: Two Vologda descriptions give the disposal of washing water a purpose, and the purposes differ. For the Middle Sukhona, an overview page says the water was poured out in a special way, with a swing, at the corner of the house, in the yard and at crossroads, and that soap used in the washing was afterwards used to calm a restless family member or a restless animal, with a formula likening them to the dead who no longer kick. S. Adonyeva, speaking of the Vologda tradition recorded in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, says that the water, washcloth and soap are destroyed so that they cannot be used in harmful magic. In one account the leftovers are a remedy, in the other a danger. The Great Russian Encyclopedia, read only in extract, calls washing an obligatory part of the rite and notes that the washing, dressing and making of the coffin may be done by specially hired people. The atlas does not decide whether the two Vologda accounts describe two beliefs or one belief told twice; it keeps both and treats the plate’s earlier statement about a prohibition around disposal as the common ground.

plates.title: THE RITUAL
plates.subtitle: Days three, nine, forty
plates.dek: The most confidently repeated ‘Russian funeral custom’ is also the one most often misdescribed: the commemoration on the third, ninth and fortieth day is a liturgical scheme before it is a folk one.
plates.marginal: The third, ninth and fortieth days are often introduced as an ancient Slavic custom. The handbook quoted on this plate is a Christian explanation of a Christian cycle; the older layer, if it exists, has not been demonstrated here.
plates.period: Liturgical sources 17th–19th c.; practice recorded 19th–21st c.
plates.tradition: Orthodox Christianity; folk elaboration

sections.heading: The shape of the forty days
paras: The commemoration of the dead on the third, ninth and fortieth day after death is set out in Orthodox handbooks, and the reasons given there are theological and not calendrical. The *Novaia Skrizhal’* (‘New Tablet’) of Archbishop Veniamin of Nizhny Novgorod (1739–1811), in its chapter of notes common to all funerals, § 2, gives more than one set. It cites Neophyte of Rhodes: the third day stands for Christ’s three days before the Resurrection, the ninth is a petition that the dead be numbered among the nine ranks of angels, and the fortieth echoes the forty days the people of Israel mourned Moses. It cites Simeon of Thessalonica, for whom the fortieth day recalls the Ascension, on the fortieth day after the Resurrection. And it adds its own reasoning: forty is a number Scripture sanctifies again and again, as in Moses’ fast, Elijah’s journey and Christ’s forty days with the apostles after the Resurrection.

The same section sets aside one explanation. Some say, it reports, that the body changes its look on the third day, decays on the ninth and that the heart itself decays by the fortieth, but these reasons ‘do not always agree with experience’. The prayers are for the forgiveness of sins and for the soul’s place among the saints and the angels. The handbook does not mention the explanations recorded in villages, that the soul visits the house for three days or is examined on the ninth. For the fortieth day, Zelenin (1927, §§ 132, 136) records that the soul was thought not yet to have left before then, and that on that day it was ‘seen off’.

sections.heading: Against the survival story
paras: Nineteenth- and early twentieth-century scholarship often read Russian funerary practice as a survival of pre-Christian religion with the Church laid over it. Zelenin (1927, § 154) writes that the bliny of Maslenitsa ‘undeniably’ show that the festival was once given to the commemoration of the dead: a reading of exactly this kind. A. K. Baiburin’s study of ritual in traditional culture, as the earlier edition summarised it and as this edition has not re-read it, treats ritual as a system of signs with its own internal logic, not as a fossil of an earlier belief, and holds that what a rite ‘originally meant’ is usually not recoverable from the surviving evidence.

This atlas therefore marks origin claims as interpretations. The forty-day cycle is documented as Christian. Whether some households also understood it as an older calendar is a question the sources used here cannot settle.

sections.heading: Who does the work: one Vologda case

meta.Role: A friend or neighbour who knows the custom; the household
meta.Evidence: Fieldwork in Vologda and Kostroma districts, 2006–2010; read from the owner’s PDF

paras: Elena Samoilova’s article on figures in North Russian funerals reports, from villages of Nyuksenitsa district in Vologda province, a ‘substitute for the dead’ that after the burial was made from the dead person’s clothing and stood in the red corner of the house until the fortieth day. Her base is field notes of 2006–2009 and O. Konshin’s notes of 1996, whose originals burned with the district centre in 2007 and were partly restored from his memory. Two accounts describe the same make-up: an undershirt rolled up, a headscarf round it, no knots, and one corner of the scarf pulled over the face. Both were made for women who died old. In one, recorded in 1996, a friend of the dead grandmother told the family to make a figure from her clothes; in the other, recorded in 2009, a neighbour said it should be seated in the corner until the fortieth day and carried out ‘when they begin to commemorate’. An informant explained the covered face: the figure ‘is not alive’.

Samoilova reads the pattern as follows. In both cases someone who knew the custom started it, not the closest kin, which she takes as a sign that the practice had passed to people who hold ritual knowledge. She offers as a working guess that a figure was made only for a respected person who died of old age. At the same time, in the district, food and water were put in front of the figure, and an informant says the plate stayed ‘until the fortieth day’. A farmer’s cloth double of his wife made in 2010 is a separate case, which she leaves open as either a revived custom or an invention. Her evidence is small: three cases for 1910–1940, from four named informants, plus the later ones. The article is read here from the owner’s PDF, pp. 251–255 and 265–268 closely, and the rest searched, not read through.

sections.heading: One calendar, many calendars
items: The dates of commemoration interact with the church calendar (the Russian Church still keeps the Julian calendar for its liturgical year, so church dates and civil dates differ). A date given in a source may not correspond to the date a family used.
Memorial days also differ by region and by parish practice. The scheme above is a frame, not a census.

sections.heading: The lament: spontaneous, and rehearsed
paras: Lamenting is the part of the ritual most often described as raw feeling. Barsov, publishing in 1872, called the laments immediate outpourings of the thoughts and feelings that loss provokes. Elena Yugai, working from interviews in several districts of Vologda Oblast with women mostly born in the 1920s–1940s, reports two kinds of lamenter in their stories: a paid specialist, and a bereaved relative who begins to lament without having planned to. The second is the one the stories are about. The same women also describe preparing: practising alone in remote places, listening closely to experienced lamenters, sometimes learning from an old woman for payment. Yugai says this training had to be kept out of sight, since the appearance of spontaneity and personal involvement belonged to the performance, and that grief itself is spoken of as the teacher.

On function she reads the laments as ritual texts with a melody that imitates weeping, addressed to the dead. At a funeral they help move the deceased into the status of an ancestor, at a commemoration they secure the protection of dead relatives, and they limit the grief of widows and orphans. This is an interpretation by one researcher, from Vologda material only, and it sets itself against both Barsov’s romantic reading and the women’s own account. The atlas keeps both: what the women say they do, and what the researcher says the rite does.

sections.heading: What the handbook says about wailing
paras: The same *Novaia Skrizhal’* (ch. XX, § 15, ‘The use of the funeral lament’) is not friendly to wailing. It says it was noticed long ago that women who, tormented by unreasoning despair, in torn clothes and with loose hair, cry out at the death of those close to them do not soften the pain but increase it and rouse others to the same weeping and praise of the dead. It recalls that the Council of Carthage forbade bishops to add their own mournful chants or eulogies to the prayers fixed by councils, and readers to use ‘wedding exclamations’ in place of church singing. The Church nevertheless allowed some mournful hymns of its own, the handbook says, to turn attention to death and the life to come, and it names the troparion sung at the end of the rite, which speaks as if with the dead person’s voice and calls friends and kin to weeping.

The passage is about ancient women’s wailing in general and about clerics who improvised; it does not name Russian peasant laments, and the atlas does not claim it was aimed at them. It does show that a handbook current in Russia from 1803 treats set church lament as acceptable and improvised lament as a fault.

plates.title: THE TABLE
plates.subtitle: Feeding the dead, feeding the living
plates.dek: The memorial meal is the place where the dead is most directly treated as a person with preferences, a place and an appetite.
plates.tradition: Orthodox memorial practice; household custom

sections.heading: The hot dinner
paras: On the day of burial everyone who came was fed. Zelenin’s survey of East Slavic ethnography (1927), § 136, explains the name of the ‘hot dinner’ (Russian *goriachii*, Belarusian *garachyi*): hot bread was always served, broken by hand and not cut with a knife, so that steam would rise. The dead were thought to need food like the living, and to feed in part on the steam from it. Ukrainians broke fresh bread in two and put it on the windowsill so that the hot steam would reach the dead.

While the dead person was still in the house they were given bliny: the first, still hot and sometimes smeared with honey, was put on the bench at the head, on the windowsill or on the shelf of icons. At the funeral and the wakes a separate place was laid for the dead, either at the common table or at a special table in the corner under the icons, and the first spoonful of any dish and the first glass of water were poured out at the corner of the table for them. The usual dishes were kutia (also kolivo, kanun), boiled barley or wheat in honey diluted with water, then bliny, honey kisel, fried eggs and porridge; the main drink was beer or braga sweetened with honey. In the Russian North, guests were given a wooden spoon after dinner in memory of the dead. Zelenin merges Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian material and cites the archive of the Russian Geographical Society by volume and number; those files were not seen, and he gives no dates.

sections.heading: Kutia, and the ambiguity of grain
paras: Kutya is boiled grain sweetened with honey, and in its church form, *kolivo*, it is brought to the memorial service and blessed. The *Novaia Skrizhal’* (1803, ch. XXIII, § 3) names boiled wheat with honey and gives the reading: the wheat that dies in the ground and then bears fruit stands for the resurrection of the dead, and the honey for the sweet, blessed life that awaits the righteous in the Kingdom of Heaven. It adds Simeon of Thessalonica’s reading of the seeds offered in the same way.

What the sources do not settle is the relationship between the church dish and the household dish. In some accounts they are the same object under two names; in others the household kutya is a separate, richer preparation with raisins or nuts. The atlas keeps both, and keeps the question open.

sections.heading: Forty days, and the table for the way home
paras: Zelenin (1927, § 136) ties several dishes to the dead person’s journey. In south Russian practice a ‘ladder’ (*lesenka*) was baked for the fortieth day, an oblong flat cake with 3, 24 or 40 cross-stripes like the steps of a stair, taken as the dead person’s climb to heaven. It was set on a bench at the gate, a requiem was sung, and the cake was then eaten with honey. Some people on that day ate bliny at the nearest crossroads, which was meant to keep the dead from finding the way home. The fortieth day is the ‘seeing off’ of the soul, and in the North a special bed was made up for the dead in the corner under the icons on the eve, so that they would rest before the long road.

Zelenin adds three items that are not Russian and are kept here as comparison. In Volhynia a bonfire was lit at the cemetery on the spring day for the dead and a common dinner cooked for all present. Belarusians on the ‘grandfathers’ days (*dziady*), the Saturdays before Maslenitsa and before St Demetrius’s day, set aside a little of each dish in a bowl by the window and poured out the first spoonful and glass with the words ‘Grandfather, come to dinner!’. Grain was scattered for birds on graves and sometimes at crossroads, which he links to the soul seen as a bird. The days of the calendar are on plate U.

Barsov’s Olonets passages put some of these items in named districts. At the funeral dinner in Ladeinopol district an empty place is left at the table in the front corner, a spoon is laid under the tablecloth and bread on top of it (1872, p. 307). On the fortieth day the relatives go out of the house to meet the priest, fully believing that the dead person is coming with him; in Brusnoe (Petrozavodsk district) a bed is made up beside the priest’s, if he arrives on the eve, for the unseen guest, and at the dinner a separate empty place with its own setting is left in the front corner while the dead person’s favourite dish is named (p. 308; the page gives no locality for the last detail). In Ladeinopol district a table with cutlery and dishes is also set on the stove for the dead, who after forty days in a cold country is said to have grown chilled and needs to warm himself (p. 309). These are local practices, and Barsov does not say how widespread any of them was.

sections.heading: Why a Ukrainian photograph is here
items: The atlas treats ‘Russian’ as a language, a state tradition and a set of institutions, not as a synonym for East Slavic. Where a photograph documents a Ukrainian or Belarusian practice, it is labelled as such.
The meal at the grave is widely attested across the region, which makes it exactly the kind of practice that gets mislabelled as ‘Russian’ by default.

sections.heading: When the table has to wait
paras: The table follows the church calendar. A reference page on the parental Saturdays states that when someone died before or during Great Lent, the commemorations on the third, ninth and fortieth days were not held in mid-week, when there is no full Liturgy, but moved to the nearest Saturday. The same page says that church rules do not regulate the memorial meal at all and offers a single guideline, moderation. The meal is therefore a custom set inside a calendar, not a rite with its own canon; the household negotiates between the two. The page names no author and describes the rule in the past tense, so the atlas uses it as a statement of the rule, not as evidence of how many households followed it.

plates.title: THE RETURNING DEAD
plates.subtitle: The unclean dead and the trouble with categories
plates.dek: Not every dead person was thought to stay dead. The distinction was not good and evil but proper and improper death — and the category that names it has been under dispute for a century.
plates.tradition: Folk belief; not church doctrine

sections.heading: Zelenin’s ‘pledged’ dead
paras: In 1916 D. K. Zelenin published a study of those who die an unnatural death — by suicide, accident, murder, drowning, or before their time — and of the rusalki. His term for them, *zalozhnye pokoiniki*, is usually translated as ‘pledged’ or ‘unclean’ dead: those whose death was not completed within the order of things.

Zelenin argued that such dead were buried apart, outside the cemetery or at its edge, in ravines, fields or at crossroads, and that they were believed to remain active — to walk, to appear, to harm. The book is a work of synthesis and it is also a work of its time, assembled from scattered reports into a system that no single informant would have recognised.

sections.heading: The dispute
paras: Later scholarship has treated Zelenin’s category with caution. The reports he gathered come from different provinces, different decades and different genres — legend, memorate, custom, ecclesiastical prohibition — and the boundary between ‘unclean’ and ‘clean’ death was drawn differently from place to place. Whether the rusalka is a development of the unclean dead, as Zelenin proposed, remains an interpretation rather than a finding.
The atlas therefore presents *zalozhnye* as a scholarly construction built on real reports, not as a folk taxonomy that everyone shared. The reports are evidence. The category is an argument.

sections.heading: Invited, fed and sent off: the dead on memorial days
paras: Svetlana Tolstaya’s 2024 article draws on published and archive collections of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and on field recordings made by her and her colleagues in Polesie (the Belarus–Ukraine borderland) in the 1960s–80s and in the Russian North and the Carpathians in the 1990s. It describes contact between the living and the dead as regulated by time, place and means, and as largely one-sided: the living perform actions, the dead are invisible and are known only by indirect signs, sounds and footprints (pp. 6–7). Her material is pan-Slavic, so the places are given below, and the Belarusian, Serbian and Slovene items are comparisons, not evidence about Russians.

For the East Slavs she lists how the dead were called on memorial days: at the gate, porch, window or door, with treats, in a high-pitched voice. A place was left at the table with a glass; a little of each dish was put aside or poured on a plate or under the table; food stayed on the table overnight; a towel was hung out so they could wash their hands; doors were not shut at night; clothes were hung in the yard for them (Slavic Antiquities, vol. 4, pp. 269–272, and her own field archive). Where the souls were not fed they were said to weep that they were hungry (vol. 2, p. 43). In Mogilev province, Belarus, people prepared a bath for the dead and, after the meal, poured water from the table to the door and told them to fly back to their place (Shein 1890, pp. 597, 609). In Polesie, on the day after the funeral, relatives took food from the memorial meal to the grave, which was called ‘waking the dead’ (field archive). In the Russian North, at the wake on the fortieth day, small children were carried round the table and asked whether they could see their father, uncle or aunt (Barsov 1997, p. 251) (pp. 6–7).

The main channel she names is dreams. The dead come to complain that the wrong clothes were put in the coffin, or that they are hungry because no memorial meal was held, or that the grave is full of water because the living wept too much, and the living respond: in one pan-Slavic account they dug up the grave to see whether the coffin was really floating (p. 8). Greetings and news for the dead could be passed in the text of a lament, which she says was common in the Russian North (Barsov 1997). She argues that this whole pattern does not sit comfortably with the usual notion of an ‘ancestor cult’: the dead are both honoured and feared, and the living feel dependent on them and anxious to keep the boundary between the two worlds (abstract, p. 1). She is one scholar, writing for a mixed Slavic sample.

Barsov records signs by which the living told whether the dead had come to a fortieth-day meal. In Samozero parish, where a table with dishes is set on the stove, they look afterwards to see whether the spoon is wet or dry. In some places in Ladeinopol district someone climbs onto the stove beforehand and looks at the table through a horse collar; a footnote from a correspondent has a close relative do this in a fur coat, looking through a sieve, and calls a sight of the dead a good sign. At Ezhessel small children are carried round the table and asked whether they see father, uncle or aunt, and if they repeat the last words, they see the unseen guest; if a bed was made up the night before, it is examined next day for creases (1872, p. 310). The next passage is a comparison, and Barsov labels it as such: among the Mordvins of two districts of Penza province, the family spreads a featherbed with the dead man’s favourite clothes in the front corner and waits for him; when he does not appear, at dawn one of his favourites goes to the grave, calls him, comes back in his likeness, bows on all sides and sits at the table, and old women ask him with deep bows whether life is good in the next world (pp. 310–311). This is a Mordvin rite, not a Russian one. The package that suggested the passage left its locality unmarked; the page does not.

sections.heading: Case notes, without the case

meta.Warning: No individual narrative is quoted here

paras: The reports share a structure: a death that violates expectation, a burial that violates place, and a subsequent sighting or disturbance. The disturbance is usually resolved by a ritual action — moving the body, reading a prayer, driving a stake, calling the priest — and the resolution tells us more about the living than about the dead.

No narrative is reproduced verbatim in this atlas. The genre is highly variable, the published texts are often retold rather than transcribed, and a single vivid quotation would misrepresent the record as more uniform than it is.

sections.heading: What the category was for
paras: The unclean dead mark the limits of the community’s obligation. They are the people for whom the full ritual was not, or could not be, performed — and the fear they provoke is the fear of an obligation left unpaid. In this reading the revenant is less a monster than an unpaid debt with a voice.
That reading is the atlas’s interpretation, offered as such. It does not require the dead to be real; it requires the living to have accounts.

sections.heading: No vampires here
items: Russian and Ukrainian records do contain stories of the dead who rise and feed, and the word *upyr’* is attested. It is a different figure from the nineteenth-century literary vampire, and the atlas does not read the one through the other.
The atlas avoids the vocabulary of horror. ‘Returning’ is a social event in these sources, not a genre.

sections.text: A bad death is the one that leaves something owing, not the one that hurts most.

sections.heading: Where the category began: Vyatka, 1909
paras: In the preface read here, Zelenin says the study did not start in a Russian village. In the summer of 1909 he surveyed the Besermyans, a small people of Vyatka province, and noted a rite he calls kuyas’kon: an offering thrown with contempt, fear and hatred to people who had died young by unnatural death, among them a miller’s wife killed in a fall from a tree, miscarried infants and murdered families of an unknown people. Seeking the same beliefs among Russians and their neighbours led him to an article of 1911 in Zhivaya starina on the cult of those dead by unnatural death among Russians and Finns, and then to the book of 1916 (Petrograd, A. V. Orlov, 328 pages). The origin matters for the plate’s dispute. The category of the ‘pledged’ dead was assembled in the first place from a non-Russian rite and extended to Russian reports, which, in the atlas’s reading, adds a reason for the caution recorded above. Only the preface was read, in a modern reissue whose editing differs from the first edition, so the atlas does not judge how far Zelenin’s extension holds.

plates.title: THE GRAVE
plates.subtitle: From churchyard to cemetery, and the architecture of a name
plates.dek: The Russian grave is a legal object before it is a sacred one. Where the dead may lie has been decided by decrees, epidemics and municipal budgets at least as often as by custom.
plates.location: Moscow, St Petersburg, Pushkin, provincial Russia
plates.tradition: Orthodox; state regulation; multi-confessional necropolises

sections.heading: The decree of 1723
paras: By a decree of Peter I dated 10 October 1723, burial in towns was restricted, with an exception for notable persons, because the churchyards at churches and monasteries had become overcrowded. Pravenc reports that the same decree ordered raised tombs levelled and relief images on shrines replaced with painted ones. A nineteenth-century account by N. P. Rozanov gives the decree this way: only ‘notable persons’ could be buried at churches in Moscow and other towns, and the rest were to go to monasteries and parish churches outside the town. He assigns the order to lower tombstones to ground level, with the inscriptions on top, to an earlier decree of 12 April 1722, and does not mention tombs or relief images in the 1723 text. One academic article dates the burial decree 16 October, not 10 October. The atlas keeps 10 October as Pravenc and Rozanov give it and treats the tombstone order as unsettled.

The measure did not last. Rozanov says the decree was not carried out because Peter died in January 1725, and that the old custom of burying at the parish churches stayed as it was under his successors. The change came in 1771, when plague struck Moscow. Rozanov names a Senate decree of 24 March 1771 that set aside special places outside the town for those who died of the disease, and one of 1 November 1771 ordering that burials at town churches stop and that cemeteries be laid out outside the towns. The article on Siberia dates a Senate decree of the same kind to 24 December 1771, and the atlas does not reconcile the dates. Vagankovo was founded in that year to receive the plague dead. The municipal note says the first burials there were unnamed Muscovites and gives no figure for the dead; popular accounts vary widely, and none is used here.

sections.heading: Out of the town, 1771–72
paras: Rozanov’s own wording for the Senate decree of 1 November 1771 is that burial at churches in towns should stop and that cemeteries be laid out outside the town on common grazing land, with small wooden churches built on them at first, at the town’s expense; places where plague victims were already buried were not to be dug up. In Moscow the cemeteries and their wooden churches were set up under the architect Bazhanov and Brigadier Durnov, who handed the consistory a register of six new churches on 31 December 1772. Vagankovo’s church of St John the Merciful is on that register. Consecration followed soon, he says, without a date in the part read. He lists six cemeteries made after the plague: Dorogomilovskoe, Vagankovskoe, Miusskoe, Pyatnitskoe, Kalitnikovskoe and Danilovskoe.

They stayed unarranged for years. Rozanov writes that the better-off were mostly buried in monasteries, that burial at the new cemeteries brought the clergy little income, and that the clergy received no money from the treasury. Of the Moscow monasteries only Spaso-Andronikov, Novospassky, Donskoy and Novodevichy kept burying. The sources read say nothing about walls, plans, registers or fees.

sections.heading: The roof over the cross
paras: The *golubets* — a cross sheltered by a small gabled roof, sometimes enclosed as a little house — is a grave form that can still be seen in Russian cemeteries. The word had a second meaning, a built-in box beside the stove in a peasant house. The roof protects the wood; it also makes the cross into a building, and the grave into a dwelling.

The atlas does not map its distribution and does not call it typical of the North: published claims about a ‘northern’ range rest on surveys this project has not consulted, and a photograph of one example is not a distribution. The word and the form come from a popular article, which is why this section stays an interpretation; Barsov’s note below is separate evidence for a small house over a grave, not for the word.

Barsov saw small houses with a roof and windows over some graves in his childhood, and in Novgorod province, in Cherepovets district, for example at Prechistaya in Andoga (1872, p. 307). The same page records that those who took part in a burial touched the stove with a hand on coming home. His note is one district; it does not give the word *golubets* and does not say how common the houses were.

sections.heading: Novodevichy Cemetery, Moscow
paras: Novodevichy Cemetery in Moscow grew up around the convent founded in the sixteenth century, as the traditional burial place of the church and noble elite of Moscow, and in the nineteenth century of the intelligentsia and merchants. A new cemetery was opened south of the convent wall in 1898, enclosed in 1898–1904 and extended in 1949. An encyclopedia entry, seen only as a search excerpt, names it as the burial place of well-known Soviet state, party and military figures, scholars, writers and actors. Rozanov, writing of the 1770s–80s, names Novodevichy among the four Moscow monasteries (with Spaso-Andronikov, Novospassky and Donskoy) where burial continued after the new cemeteries were opened.

Two examples recorded in the photographs used by this atlas: the grave of Ilya Ilf, and a double monument for the writer A. N. Stepanov and his wife, designed — according to the photographer’s description — as two ships on a dark sea. The atlas repeats that description as a description, not as a documented intention of the family.

sections.heading: Portraits on stone
items: Photographic portraits set into headstones are a familiar feature of late-Soviet and post-Soviet cemeteries. The atlas has not found a scholarly source for their chronology and does not date them here.
The same caution applies to the enamel photograph, the plastic wreath and the metal fence: visible everywhere, documented in the sources used here almost nowhere.

sections.heading: Tobolsk: closed ground, an old man’s request, two infants
paras: The law of the cemetery reached Siberia as paperwork. A Senate decree of 24 December 1771 banned burial at town parish churches and called for new ground outside the town; the Tobolsk consistory applied it to villages of its eparchy, and in 1783 the parish of Abalak was moved to Preobrazhenskoye while the old church complex became a monastery. Lay burial at Abalak stopped. In August 1815, though, a peasant of Abalak volost, Alexey Vakhrushev, was buried inside the monastery enclosure after a service by a priest of the Preobrazhenskaya church, without the knowledge of the local authorities. The abbot said the elderly man, ill with tuberculosis and asthma, had asked for it before he died. The gubernia board wanted exhumation; more than twenty days had passed, and sanitary risk prevented it. A Synod decree of 12 April 1833 later allowed burial in closed cemeteries in exceptional cases, such as priests and large donors, and in 1912–13 the consistory reviewed 19 petitions for burial within church or monastery enclosures and refused one.

The law also had a smaller edge. Stillborn and unbaptized children could lie in general cemeteries but without rites or commemoration. At the abandoned village of Yarkova, in the Tobolsk district, archaeologists in 2015 opened a 50 m² trench in a garden plot beside a cliff and found two children’s burials of the mid-nineteenth to early twentieth century, in logs, shallow, with twisted cords and some factory cloth. With no other graves nearby, the authors read it as a household plot for unbaptized infants. That is their reading, from two burials, and the sources do not say which of two long-settled families used it.

plates.title: THE VOICE
plates.subtitle: Lament, euphemism, and the grammar of address
plates.dek: The dead are spoken to. The grammar of that address is one of the most precisely recorded things in Russian ethnography — and one of the least often quoted accurately.
plates.location: Olonets province (Karelia) and the Russian North
plates.tradition: Folk lament; Orthodox liturgical language

sections.heading: Barsov’s volumes: who laments for whom
paras: The first volume of E. V. Barsov’s *Prichitaniia Severnogo kraia* (Moscow, 1872) arranges its funeral laments by the relationship between the dead person and the one who laments: a widow for her husband comes first (printed p. 1), then a daughter for her father and for her mother, laments for a wife, a son, a daughter, a goddaughter, a brother, a sister, uncles and cousins, and then for the drowned (p. 252), for a drunkard (p. 271), for a village elder, a clerk and a priest (p. 293). The headings and page numbers are taken from the contents page of the Internet Archive scan, as machine-read OCR, and have not been collated with a paper copy.

In the introduction Barsov separates the professional lamenter from the household in mourning: the people, he writes, produce figures who long remain carriers of the old funeral lament, known as *voplenitsy*; he also notes that whole villages sometimes gather to pay the dead their last duty (pp. II–III).

A lament has no fixed text of the kind an epic song has. Kuznetsova and Kovyrshina (Petrozavodsk, 2000) describe a local ‘school’ of lamenters as a shared stock of obligatory motifs, formulas, compositional patterns and melodies, learned informally from childhood by girls who watched village weddings and acted them out in play. Their example is from Vyrozero in the Zaonezhye: an ordinary performer’s wedding lament runs to some 40–50 lines, Fedosova’s lament at the handclasp to 1,074. That figure belongs to a wedding lament, not a funeral one; it shows how far a single performer could lengthen a text by improvising between formulas.

sections.heading: A funeral day in laments, as Vologda performers describe it
paras: Elena Iugai’s study draws on funeral laments of the eastern part of Vologda province, published by B. Efimenkova (1980) and by Iugai herself (2011), and begins with a warning: the Olonets laments of Barsov’s volumes are not representative of all Russian laments, because his informants Fedosova, Bogdanova and Pashkova were not ordinary lament-singers, their texts being very long and rich; a fair picture needs a large corpus of smaller texts, such as those from the Novgorod region (Berdyaeva 2015) and the South Urals (Rozhkova and Moiseeva 2008) (p. 166). She says that in pre-revolutionary Russia laments were an obligatory part of the funeral, with different types for different stages, and that the genre has since lost that role (p. 167).

The performers’ own names for laments mark moments: ‘when he is lying on the bench’, ‘when they carry the coffin’, ‘in the cemetery’, the last covering laments at the digging of the grave, at the anniversary and on visits to the cemetery on Trinity Saturday. On the day of burial, as she describes it, relatives lament in the house of the dead while guests lament on their way to it. The text narrates a search: the performer wakes, washes, looks for the dead person in the yard and the house, finds him in the red corner and reproaches his silence. When the helpers close the coffin she laments again, asking them not to. The full ‘parting in the house’ can run to hundreds of lines. On the way to the cemetery the dead says farewell to the house, the street, the village, the forests and the whole world; at the cemetery the lament soothes the dead, whose relatives are waiting for him; a last lament is sung on the way back (pp. 167–168).

Informants separate these from commemoration laments, which are more symbolic, less improvised and closer to lyrical songs, and which can be sung within the first 39 days (on the ninth or twentieth), on the fortieth day, at the anniversary, on feast days or on any day. The soul is thought to come to the commemoration feast: in some Vologda villages a table is laid for the souls and a clean towel hung out for them to wash their hands, and a lament invites them. In the west of the province there is a lament inviting the dead to the bath; in the east the bath is prepared but no lament belongs to it. Today, she says, a performer often knows only one short lament, built from the traditional formulas, and uses it both at funerals and at commemorations (pp. 168–169). This is one author’s description of one region; it does not say how widely the same sequence held elsewhere.

Barsov’s own note on the funeral dinner shows the laments as an order of performance. In the Olonets passage that puts the dead person’s table on the stove (Ladeinopol district), the lamenters begin at the first dish, first lamenting to the priest and the clergy, then to relatives, neighbours and outsiders present; they walk through the house, bow to the four corners and lament at every place where the dead person sat, lay and walked, then go out to the barn, the yard and, if near, the fields. The sequence repeats after the second and third dishes, the lamenters change after each, and the priest is seen off with tears in the belief that the dead goes back to the cemetery with him (1872, p. 309). Barsov’s introduction also records what church and state made of lamenting. It quotes the Stoglav Council of 1551, which complained that on Trinity Saturday men and women at the graves wept with great shouting and, when buffoons and musicians began to play, stopped weeping to dance and sing ‘satanic songs’, and told priests to turn their flocks from these ‘pagan customs’ (ch. 4, q. 23); and a decree of 1715 in which Peter I, on the death of Tsaritsa Marfa Matveevna, ordered that no one should give such indecent howling over her or over any other dead person. Barsov says the decree touched the Westernised upper layer and had no influence on the mass of the people, and adds that Peter’s own coffin was lamented in a folk lament (pp. VIII–IX). Both are quoted at second hand, and ‘pagan’ is the Council’s word, not a finding.

sections.heading: Occasions, not a score

meta.Form: Performed, formulaic, address in the second person

paras: Barsov’s introduction ties laments to successive occasions: the moment of dying, the burial, and later visits when the mourner speaks to the dead and invites them back into the house. The passage ranges over several pages (about pp. V–XVI) and the individual pages have not been collated.

The six-part movement of address, question about the road, complaint, self-reproach, description of the grave and farewell, which an earlier version of this plate presented ‘after Barsov’, is the atlas’s own working schema. It was not checked against the printed laments and is withdrawn as a statement about Barsov’s texts.

sections.heading: The second person
paras: Russian funerary language keeps the dead in the second person and in the present tense for as long as the ritual lasts. The dead is addressed by kin term — ‘my child’, ‘my master’, ‘my sister’ — and asked questions that presume an answer. The euphemisms that surround death in ordinary speech (*ushel* — ‘he has gone’; *ne stalo* — ‘he is no more’) are suspended in the lament, where the dead is named and spoken to directly. This is an interpretive reading carried over from the earlier edition. It has not yet been checked against lament texts and stands as unverified until it is.

sections.heading: Fedosova, and the question of the author
paras: Most of the laments in Barsov’s volumes were recorded from one woman, Irina Andreevna Fedosova (1827–1899), a lamenter from the Zaonezhye north of Lake Onega; a few were added later from her by O. Kh. Agreneva-Slavianskaia. Kuznetsova and Kovyrshina place her birth in a village of the Vyrozero district (née Yulina) and her later life at Kuzarand; her melodies were noted between 1886 and 1895 by Agreneva-Slavianskaia, S. G. Rybakov and N. A. Rimsky-Korsakov, and a phonograph recording of 1896 by Yu. I. Blok was transcribed and published much later. Reference works disagree on her birth year, 1827 or 1831, and this atlas follows the 1827 given in the scholarly articles read. The consequence for the plate is concrete. A genre described above as formulaic and communal reaches us largely through a single, exceptionally skilled voice, recorded by outsiders, in a setting that was not a funeral. Philologists have debated how much of the printed text is the tradition and how much is the performer. The sources read here do not allow the atlas to settle that, and it does not.

Fedosova was not the only named voice. In the register of performers that closes the first volume, Barsov lists five women, and the lament printed there as No. XI comes from a peasant woman of the village of Tverdilovo, Kalyazin uyezd, Tver province, Klavdiya Momokova, who by his account learned to lament in her own village while still unmarried and was living in Moscow when he wrote. Another, Anna Perventseva, was a priest’s daughter who learned at the churchyard on Sundays and feast days; a third, Marya Fedorova of Kargopol, a deacon’s daughter, learned from an old lamenter who had taken shelter in her parents’ house. The portraits are Barsov’s own, selective and at times unfriendly, and give no recording dates; they show that the collection rests on named women of different standing, not on an anonymous “people”.

plates.title: THE AFTERLIFE
plates.subtitle: Doctrine, image, and the soul’s itinerary
plates.dek: Orthodox teaching about the dead is precise, and it is not the same thing as the crowded cosmology of the icon. The atlas keeps the two apart, then puts them on the same page.
plates.period: Iconography 15th–18th c.; doctrine and practice to the present
plates.tradition: Orthodox Christianity; folk elaboration

sections.heading: What the Church says
paras: Orthodox teaching holds that the dead are judged and that the living may pray for them. The funeral rites ask for the forgiveness of sins and for a place ‘with the saints’; memorial services repeat the request at intervals. The fortieth day is the last of the appointed commemorations; the annual commemoration continues after it.

The Church’s language is deliberately restrained about the intermediate state. Where popular literature supplies a detailed itinerary — where the soul goes on which day, what it sees — the atlas marks that as devotional or folk elaboration, not as doctrine.

sections.alt: A large eighteenth-century Russian icon of the Last Judgment, densely painted with registers of saints, angels, scales, a river of fire and compartments of punishment
sections.caption: The Last Judgment. Volga region, 1770s–1780s. Tempera on wood, 180 × 137 cm. The icon is dense with inscribed texts and compartments; it is a picture that expects to be read.

sections.heading: Reading the icon
paras: The Last Judgment icon is a diagram as much as a painting. Christ appears in glory; the scales weigh souls; the righteous move toward the heavenly city; the damned descend into a river of fire; the punishments are arranged in small compartments, each with its own inscription and its own social type — the miser, the adulterer, the usurer, the drunkard.

The Volga icon used here belongs to the eighteenth century and to the urban artisan milieu: it borrows heavily from printed engravings, including their page-like blocks of text. Its text blocks and compartments follow printed models, so it was made for viewers who read.

sections.heading: A narrative that is not a dogma
paras: The best-known popular itinerary of the soul in Russia comes from one text: the vision of Theodora in the Life of St Basil the New. In it the dead woman appears to Basil’s disciple Gregory and describes how angels escorted her through a series of trials, at which evil spirits tried to claim her soul for its sins. According to the Orthodox Encyclopedia, as cited in a Russian theological article, the Life was written in Constantinople in the second half of the tenth century and exists in several redactions. The same article states that the toll-house narrative became widely accepted but never acquired the status of a binding dogma of the Church, and reads its images as parable-like language, not as literal topography. The atlas takes the distinction from that article: the narrative is documented as hagiography and widely received; its status as doctrine is disputed in the very source that defends it. The article was read, not the Life itself, so no list of the trials is given here.

plates.title: COLLECTIVE DEATH
plates.subtitle: Plague, war, and the state’s arithmetic of the dead
plates.dek: Mass death produces two things at once: a hole in the record and an official number. The atlas is interested in the gap between them.
plates.marginal: At Piskaryovskoye the count is given as about 470,000 in some accounts and about 520,000 in others. The gap is no rounding error: the two figures count different things.
plates.tradition: State commemoration; Orthodox and secular rites

sections.heading: 1771: the pit
paras: The Moscow plague of 1771 killed in the tens of thousands. The dead were buried outside the city, and the new cemetery at Vagankovo received, first of all, unnamed people. The historical account of the cemetery begins with a number it cannot disaggregate.
Mass death produces this kind of record: a pit, a total, a name for the place, no names for the people. The atlas does not illustrate the pit. It prints the fact of it.

sections.heading: The unknown soldier
paras: The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Kremlin wall was opened on 8 May 1967. The monument was designed by the architects Dmitrii Burdin, Vladimir Klimov and Iurii Rabaev, with the sculptor Nikolai Tomskii; the remains had been brought from a mass grave outside Moscow. The eternal flame was lit at the opening and has been maintained since.

The unknown soldier is a very specific solution to a problem of scale: it converts an unmanageable number into a single body that can be visited. What it gains in ritual focus it loses in information. The state’s memory is built on that trade.

sections.heading: Unburied
paras: Alexander Etkind’s *Warped Mourning* argues that Soviet culture was shaped by deaths that were not buried properly — the executed, the disappeared, the dead in unmarked ground — and that literature and memory-work in Russia have repeatedly returned to them as the ‘undead’. The argument is a cultural history, not a survey of graves, and the atlas presents it as an interpretation.

Catherine Merridale’s *Night of Stone* makes a related point from the side of the living: the twentieth century in Russia produced so much death that mourning itself became a skill that had to be managed, suppressed, or performed in private. Both books are used here for their arguments, not as inventories of fact.

sections.heading: ‘Buried well’: a village formula and the funeral photograph
paras: Oleg Nikolaev, a philologist at the Memorial society, wrote in 2012 about funeral photographs in Russian family albums. From his fieldwork he reports that in some archives they make up to 20% of all pictures, and that they peak in the 1950s–1970s: at the open coffin, on the lorry to the cemetery, at the grave, at the memorial table. He thinks the practice belongs to villages, small provincial towns and city people of village origin, and that it had largely left use by the 1980s (pp. 358–359, 361, 369–370). The two photographs reproduced in the article come from family archives in Bashkortostan and the Chelyabinsk region (pp. 359–360).

His central observation is a phrase. In the stories he collected, a funeral is judged by the formula ‘buried well’ (*pokhoronili khorosho*), and a story often begins or ends with it. It covers correct ritual from washing to the memorial meal, a good place near relatives, a tended grave, telegrams sent to the family and many people coming to take leave, and also that the grief was told and heard (p. 365). He found the same phrase in a soldier’s letter of 25 September 1943, where a comrade tells a widow that her husband was buried well and that the grave was edged with turf and a marker set up; the letter is held in the digital archive of the ‘Museum of Folk Writing’ programme (p. 368).

From this he argues that the photograph served the same formula in visual form. His reasoning: after the war, deportation and the camps many families knew of relatives who had gone missing or lain in mass or nameless graves, and a photograph proved that this family could bury its own dead, and bury them correctly. Prints were sent to relatives in other towns, which let a scattered kin group see who stood by the coffin (pp. 368–369). This is his hypothesis, put forward as a supposition, and it rests on his own expedition collections, which the article does not list or count. The plate uses it as an interpretation beside Etkind and Merridale, and does not treat it as a measured fact.

sections.heading: Trinity Saturday at a mass grave: Yurla district, Perm region, 2013–2015
paras: A team from Perm State University (Svetlana Koroleva, Elena Chetina, Oksana Kolegova) gathered interviews and photographs in the Yurla district of the Perm region, a Russian-speaking area among Komi-Permyaks, in 2013–2015. Their article describes how places linked to the Civil War and to the settling of special deportees (1919 to the early 1950s) came into local commemoration. Their finding is that the places fall on a spectrum between official and popular forms, and that where the popular form prevails the mass grave is placed in the calendar commemoration of one’s own dead, which turns from a family rite into a shared one.

Their clearest case is Ust-Pyshya, a logging settlement founded in the late 1940s or early 1950s that ceased to exist in 2014. Until then its residents held a multi-stage commemoration in Trinity week: first the graves of their relatives at the cemetery near the village of Bulychi, then the obelisk at the mass grave of fourteen people shot there by Whites in 1919, whose names are mostly unknown, and then a cemetery of Polish special settlers, always in nearly the same order. All informants the authors spoke to said they went to the grave on Trinity Saturday and not on revolutionary holidays. They censed their own relatives’ graves, then those of people with no one to commemorate, then the obelisk, brought food, and called the dead simply the ‘killed’. One woman explained the visits by saying that nobody else commemorated them. The authors also report that other Yurla places linked to bloodshed or abandoned cemeteries were understood as ‘unclean’ and dangerous.

The evidence is interview recollection in one district, with the authors’ own count of informants not stated in the part read, and the narrators of the mythological stories are withheld by the authors’ own note. It shows a documented case of an ordinary calendar rite extended to the war dead of a settlement that no longer exists. It cannot tell how common the practice is in Russia; the plate keeps it beside Nikolaev’s village formula as a second regional observation.

sections.heading: Why there are no bodies here
items: This plate uses no photographs of corpses, no photographs of starving people, no images of the blockade dead. The atlas treats these as deaths, not as imagery.
The monuments are shown because they are what the state built, and because their surfaces are evidence of how memory was organised.

sections.heading: Butovo: a count with four numbers
paras: The Butovo firing range south of Moscow is the plate’s case of mass death that was administered, not suffered by accident. A memorial site run by the church says it is the largest place of mass shootings and burials of victims of Stalinist repression in the Moscow region, that 20,760 names are known, that the shootings fell between August 1937 and October 1938, and that the range worked from 1934 to 1953. The Great Russian Encyclopedia, read only in extract, gives about 20.8 thousand executed and buried in those months, of them 19.9 thousand men, over 80 per cent non-party. Other pages read give 20,761, 20,762 and 20,765. The atlas does not choose among them. The spread is small. The figure rests on execution lists and case files, so it exists because the state kept records, the reverse of the 1771 pit. No remains are shown.

sections.heading: The procession of portraits
paras: Collective death is also remembered from below, and the best-documented recent case began in Siberia. According to Meduza, on 9 May 2012 six thousand people in Tomsk walked with portraits of their relatives who fought in the war; the form was taken up in about 140 places in 2013 and about 450 in 2014. The same article is mainly about a dispute over who owns the name and the procession, which this plate does not follow. What matters here is the object: a photograph carried on a stick through a city, one dead person to one living carrier. It is the opposite of the unknown soldier earlier on this plate, which merges many into one; here the many are kept apart, each with a face and a relative.

plates.title: DEATH IN ART
plates.subtitle: The sled, the black square, and the deathbed as an argument
plates.dek: Russian art tends to approach death through a single object held at an angle: a coffin on a sled, a square on a wall, a body on a bed.
plates.tradition: Painting, literature, the avant-garde

sections.heading: Perov, 1865
paras: Vasily Perov’s *Seeing Off the Dead* (*Provody pokoinika*, 1865; oil on canvas, 45.3 × 57 cm; Tretyakov Gallery, inv. 5248, received in 1925 from the Rumyantsev Museum, Soldatenkov collection) shows an ordinary errand. A thin horse pulls a sled up a snowy road. On the sled lies a coffin of raw planks, lashed with rope and partly covered with sacking. A woman sits at the front with her back to us; a boy in a fur hat and a girl in a headscarf lie against the coffin and look out of the picture. A dog stands on the road behind the sled. No one else is there.

The sky is low and dark, the road bare, with a strip of spruce on the right. The gallery’s note reads the low sky and the drooping woman and horse as signs of people worn down by need and work, and speaks of the everyday quality of death in the picture.

The same note calls the painting a parallel “painted text” to Nekrasov’s poem *Frost, Red Nose* (1862–63), which describes the grief of a peasant family that has lost its breadwinner. Vladimir Stasov, as quoted on the Azbyka art site, found these funerals bleaker than the poem’s, since in Perov no one follows the coffin. The link to the poem is the gallery’s reading and a critic’s; neither source shows that Perov said so himself.

sections.heading: The deathbed as a room
paras: Three Russian prose works about dying sit here as a reading list, not as evidence: Tolstoy’s *The Death of Ivan Ilyich* (1886), Chekhov’s *The Death of a Clerk* (1883) and Bunin’s *The Gentleman from San Francisco* (1915). In Tolstoy a dying man passes through pain and denial to an opening at the very end. In Chekhov a clerk dies of embarrassment. In Bunin a rich American dies in a hotel and the story gives his death no dignity.
The pairing is the atlas’s own reading. Each author uses a death to test the social order, and the results differ.

sections.heading: The square that was a gravestone
paras: Kazimir Malevich died in Leningrad on 15 May 1935. His body was cremated in Moscow, and the urn was buried at Nemchinovka on 21 May 1935. Novaya Gazeta says it was lowered into a shallow pit under a large old oak; Moskovsky Komsomolets places the grave under a lone oak in the ‘Romashkovo field’. A wooden cube made by Nikolai Suetin, with a black square on one side, was set on the spot, and a board nailed to the oak named the great artist whose ashes lay there. The Stedelijk log describes a family photograph of 1935 beside the cube; it is not reproduced here.

What followed rests on one newspaper account. Novaya Gazeta writes that Malevich’s name was banned from 1937, that the oak was felled in 1941 for defensive works, that in 1944 relatives found only the stump and the brick base of the cube, and that in the 1950s the roots were dug out and the field sown. Moskovsky Komsomolets says the grave was lost and the cube vanished, and that a replacement cube set up in 1988 had a red square. A house was later built on the burial site, according to Radio Svoboda, and in 2015 the authors of the Novaya Gazeta article reported a ground-penetrating radar survey that, they say, settled the location; that claim is theirs and was not checked here. The sources read do not say what became of the cube itself.

sections.heading: On not illustrating grief
items: No literary quotations appear on this plate. Passages describing dying are easy to excerpt and hard to excerpt honestly.
The Perov painting is shown whole. The halftone is the atlas’s own treatment of it.

sections.heading: The coffin as an art object
paras: The funeral that preceded the burial was itself made as art, but the accounts disagree on details. Novaya Gazeta describes a Suprematist coffin, a truck with a black square on its radiator driving along Nevsky Prospect, and a railway car to Moscow, where the body was cremated at the Donskoy crematorium. The Thyssen museum credits Nikolai Suetin with decorating the coffin with Suprematist motifs and organising the funeral. The Stedelijk log says the pupils Konstantin Rozhdestvensky and Nikolai Suetin designed it, not Malevich, a belief it calls a legend with some basis; it describes the coffin as green, black and white, with a red circle at the feet and a black square at the head, and says the cross was left out to avoid religious reference. Novaya Gazeta says the opposite on the cross: it states that Malevich asked for a cross-shaped coffin and that his friends and pupils made one with a cross at the end. That statement rests on the article alone and conflicts with the Stedelijk account. The atlas therefore keeps only what the sources share, a Suprematist coffin made by his circle with Suetin’s hand in it, and leaves the cross open. Photographs of the body, in a coffin the log calls architecton-shaped, are described in the log; none is reproduced here.

sections.alt: Hand-coloured woodcut: a warrior with a sword and spear on a blue horse, a fallen figure beneath the horse, and at the right a thin figure with a scythe and a quiver of arrows, with lines of Slavonic text above
sections.caption: ‘Anika the Warrior and Death’, a hand-coloured woodcut lubok, 17th century (State Historical Museum, as given on Commons). Death appears as a thin figure with a scythe and a quiver, facing a mounted warrior; a figure lies under the horse. A popular tale in pictures, not a record of any rite, and an early case of how death was drawn for a wide public.

sections.alt: Black-and-white printed plate of a long lubok in three strips: rows of mice with sticks, carts and drums lead a procession in which a large cat lies on a sledge, with numbered scenes and several columns of printed text below

Mice lead a funeral procession with the cat on a sledge. It is a joke in the form of a funeral, so it shows what a procession looked like to the people who bought it, not how any burial was done. What it mocks is not discussed here.

plates.title: THE SOVIET AFTERLIFE
plates.subtitle: Cremation, the civil funeral, and the industry that followed
plates.dek: Civil funerals without a priest, cremation in a former church, and a funeral market, seen mostly through Moscow sources.
plates.tradition: State secular ritual; Orthodox revival; commercial funeral services

sections.heading: A crematorium in a church
paras: Moscow’s first crematorium was fitted into a church building at the Donskoy Monastery, the church of St Seraphim of Sarov and St Anna of Kashin. A Moscow city-guide page calls it an unfinished church never consecrated before the revolution; an Orthodox website calls it a rebuilt church. A design competition was held by the Moscow communal administration in 1925, according to a 1926 magazine as quoted on an archive site, and a hobbyist page names Dmitry Osipov as the architect of the conversion. The furnace, the Orthodox site writes, came from the German firm Topf and Sons.

The dates differ by a day or so. Sokolova gives 12 January 1927 as the opening; the hobbyist page gives a trial burning of a worker’s body on 11 January. The official opening is 6 October 1927 in the Memorial database and the archive site, 7 October on the hobbyist page.

The building was later used for the terror. Memorial’s Topos database records that bodies of people shot in Moscow were cremated at Donskoy, documented from 1934, with earlier cases possible, and that the ashes were buried in the New Donskoy cemetery.

sections.heading: The civil funeral
paras: A Soviet funeral had no priest. In the 1920s the ‘red funeral’ was a procession to the cemetery led by musicians, with Komsomol members carrying a red coffin, then flags and revolutionary songs, and at the grave a civil memorial service with an honour guard and speeches. Sokolova concludes that such funerals were rare in the 1920s, the political act of a narrow circle of young activists.

Her figures: in Moscow, 39.9% of funerals in 1925 and 40.4% in 1926 were held without a church service, so about six in ten still had one; in Tambov province, nine civil funerals in the first quarter of 1927 for the whole province. She writes that the 1960s brought a state campaign for socialist non-religious rites, with local commissions, and that funeral rites appear in only some of its guideline collections. The article was read in summary only.

sections.heading: The funeral market, Moscow 1996–2012
paras: The federal law of 12 January 1996 ‘On Burial and Funeral Business’ guarantees relatives a list of burial services free of charge, provided by a specialised service (Article 9). In June 2012, The Moscow Times reports, the head of the city’s trade and services department said commercial burial functions, such as delivering the body, coffins and gravestones, would pass from the municipal company Ritual to private firms. The same report puts the Moscow burial-services market at more than 12 billion rubles, cremation at 44% of Moscow burials, and the number of cemeteries at 71, only two of them open to new burials.

These are Moscow figures from one newspaper report and say nothing about the rest of Russia. The sources read do not cover the years 1991–95 or after 2012, and they do not show how church funerals returned.

sections.heading: A temple of atheism, then a plant
paras: A.D. Sokolova’s study of 1920s cremation argues that in the USSR the decision on disposing of the dead passed to the civil authorities, who started from sanitation. Even so, the first project, in Petrograd, was called a ‘Crematorium-Temple’ and aimed at creating a spiritual mood in the masses. By the second half of the decade, when the Donskoy crematorium was built in Moscow, her abstract says, the technology had come to matter more than the quasi-religious dress. The later history is thinner. A records entry describes the Nikolo-Arkhangelsk crematorium in east Moscow, completed in March 1972, with seven twin cremators and six halls of farewell. A hobbyist page says the Donskoy furnace closed in 1973 and was rebuilt as a church in 1990; a Moscow guide page agrees only that it stopped working in the 1970s and that the church received the main building in the 1990s. The atlas does not settle the year.

sections.kicker: PART I · THE HOUSE AT A DEATH
sections.heading: A house that has been broken
paras: Maria Andryunina’s survey of Ukrainian, Belarusian, western Russian and Polish funeral rites reports that at a death doors and windows were opened and holes made in the roof or ceiling, so that death could come in and the soul go out. By her account the house was then treated as broken. Its sacred boundaries were annulled, and an unsettled soul could haunt it, which made it dangerous for the living.

The corpus matters. The rites in that article come from the western and southern fringes of the Eastern Slavic world and from Poland, and the plate does not offer them as a single Russian custom. The same article reports the reverse for new buildings: a newly built house counted as incomplete until the first death within it.
