sections.heading: The window
paras: Jelena Lewkijewskaja’s study of the window in the traditional culture of the Eastern Slavs treats it as a ritual entrance and exit between this world and the other. In funeral rites and in legends about death it is the route by which the souls of the dead, and mythological figures, enter and leave the house. Throwing something out of a window is a way of disposing of a dangerous or impure thing. In the same tradition a house without windows is the dwelling of someone alien, a being from another world.

Put beside the open windows of the deathbed, this gives a dwelling whose openings are working parts of the rite. The study is five pages long and generalises across all the Eastern Slavs, and only its abstract was available to the atlas. It frames the question; it does not describe any one village.

sections.kicker: PART II · THE COFFIN AS A HOUSE
sections.heading: The coffin as a house
paras: Anna Plotnikova’s essay on the earthly places of death starts from the Slavic idea of death as a passage to another world, where the dead acquire a home. The coffin, the grave and the graveyard are read as that home’s earthly forms. A coffin is sometimes built like a house, with window openings, and its inside can copy a living home: an icon corner, bedding, everyday things. Funeral laments call it a cold, dark house without windows, and some words for ‘coffin’ derive from the word for ‘house’.

On the same reading the dead remain tied to the home they left, and funeral customs work at separating them from it, by changing the route out of the house or by removing the dead person’s belongings. The essay covers Slavic traditions broadly. Which of these details are recorded for Russian regions has not yet been traced, and the bibliographic record for the essay is incomplete (see the source note).

sections.heading: A written prayer left in a house that is being abandoned, 2015–2017
paras: Andrei Moroz, a folklorist, describes three cases he came across in fieldwork in 2015, 2016 and 2017, and a hypothesis drawn from them. In July 2015 an informant in the Velsk district of Arkhangelsk region showed the expedition of the Russian State University for the Humanities a village where a grass fire had burned all the houses except two. He said that in the house of an absent neighbour he had found handwritten sheets of a protective prayer lying on a sideboard, and that the fire had turned aside at that house. Moroz did not see these sheets, since the informant’s wife refused to show them, but at the house he saw two sheets of copied prayers on a bench. In July 2016 a Higher School of Economics expedition in the Zlynka district of Bryansk region, which lies in the Chernobyl contamination zone, was shown an emptied house sold to the state, with a floor taken up and the stove half fallen, where a small note with a short protective formula lay on a corner table in the kitchen. In July 2017 Moroz and colleagues searched abandoned houses in Malaya Shalga, Kargopol district, and found in one a stitched notebook with a herdsman’s spell, on the ledge of the cupboard that divides the room.

What the three had in common, he says, was that the houses were left for good or for a long time, that a handwritten sacred text lay in the open, that each text had the stated function of a charm, and that each lay in the middle of the living part of the house, near the cross-beam (*matitsa*) that divides it. He ties the practice to the migration of villagers to towns and the use of village houses as summer homes, and he adds that two summer residents in Sudroma kept charms against thieves in hidden places by the door. He says openly that the practice may be new, that the answers for the Chernobyl house are unclear, and that how widespread it is has not been investigated, since no interviews have been done with people who leave their houses for long periods (the article, in the journal *Kultura slavian i kultura evreev: dialog, skhodstva, razlichiia*, 2019).

sections.kicker: M / LIVING IN A DYING VILLAGE
sections.heading: A forest settlement seen by its older residents, 2018
paras: T. V. Zhigaltsova, a psychologist, mapped how older residents see the logging settlement of Komsomolsky in the Velsk district of Arkhangelsk region, from 32 questionnaires and 10 interviews with people aged 50 and over. The settlement is called abandoned in the title, yet people still live in it, and the article says that most respondents wanted to move and all called their stay forced, while describing the settlement as their ‘life’, ‘birthplace’ and ‘home’. Places that awoke pity included the empty school (28.1% of answers), abandoned houses (15.6%) and the hospital (12.5%); among places that cause shame, the unsanctioned rubbish dump had 21%.

The cemetery appears in the answers twice. One respondent named it among the settlement’s sad places together with ‘the dying’ of the settlement, and the shame list includes ‘abandoned graves in the cemetery’; one person writes that they would move to ‘the graves of ancestors’, near relatives. The map places the cemetery and the dump outside the settlement’s physical bounds, in the zone of negative feeling. This is one settlement and a small sample, the questionnaire design is the author’s, and the article does not ask what the residents believe about the dead; it supports only that, in one northern settlement, an untended grave counts as part of what is felt to have gone wrong.

sections.heading: Fourteen settlements abolished in north-eastern Karelia, 1938–2005
paras: A 2023 article by O. A. Balabeikina, V. Yu. Korobushchenko and A. A. Mazurenko (*Vestnik Pskovskogo gosudarstvennogo universiteta*, vol. 16, no. 1, pp. 3–12) counts the settlements formally abolished in four districts of the Republic of Karelia: Loukhi, Kem, Belomorsk and Segezha. They found 14 between 1938 and 2005, working from legislative decisions, municipal sites and photographs and recollections posted online. They note that Russian law lets a settlement be abolished by an administrative act, with a low population (under 100), low density and poor transport access among the usual criteria (Federal Law no. 131-FZ, art. 13), and that in almost every case the territory was simply joined to a neighbouring rural settlement. The exceptions they name are Soroka, which became part of the town of Belomorsk, and Yuma, which was flooded: its residents were moved by 1989 for the Krivoporozhskaya hydropower station.

Two items bear on the dead. At Pulozero, in Belomorsk district, they list the remains of ruined houses, a chapel and ‘necro-cult structures’ on the cemetery, together with a cult grove; the settlement had 52 inhabitants in 1905. And for Petrovsky Yam in Segezha district, abolished in 1982, they report that a Finnish sabotage group destroyed hospital no. 2212 of the Karelian Front on 12 February 1942, and that a public group has held a ‘Memory Escort’ there for several decades, on dates near the anniversary, riding 70 km by snowmobile over the frozen Lake Vygozero from Segezha. The article does not give numbers of graves, residents or visitors. It shows that an abolition is a legal fact, and that the places can still draw a visit around an anniversary because of the dead.

sections.heading: What an uninhabited village is, and is not
items: A village counted as uninhabited has no registered residents at the census. The figure does not say whether its houses still stand, who owns them or whether anyone returns in summer. The three reports count three different things, and the atlas does not turn them into a number of empty houses. The Rosstat tables were not consulted, only reports of them.

Only one source used here records a practice in abandoned houses in Russian regions: Moroz’s three cases of protective texts left behind, which he presents as a possibly new practice of unknown spread. Zhigaltsova records feelings about abandoned houses, not beliefs. The ritual material of parts I and II concerns houses in which someone has died, not houses that were left. Whether the two connect is a research lead, not a finding.

plates.title: THE FOREST EDGE
plates.subtitle: Burial away from the churchyard, the forest on the road to the dead, and a hut at the border
plates.dek: Four kinds of evidence put the dead near the forest: reports of burial in forest ravines, a belief that the way to the dead leads through the woods, a fairy-tale hut at the treeline, and a 1927 survey of the forest spirit. They come from different peoples and different genres, and the plate does not blend them.
plates.marginal: One report is about Mordvins. One article is mostly Estonian and Belarusian. One is a reading of folktales. One is a single compiler’s survey of the 1920s. None of them is a map of where Russians buried anyone.
plates.location: Saratov and Simbirsk provinces (reports); Estonia and Belarus (corpus); Russian folktales (reading)
plates.tradition: Eastern Slavic and neighbouring folk belief

sections.heading: A report from Simbirsk province
paras: Dmitry Zelenin’s 1916 essays on those who died an ‘unnatural’ death are a compilation of local reports, made by other people and gathered into one book. Two are used on this plate; this part takes the first. In Silinskaya volost, Simbirsk guberniya, a ‘deaf forest ravine’ was held to be the proper grave for someone who had drunk himself to death, and burial in the cemetery was said to bring drought and crop failure.

It is a report in someone else’s book, read here through an excerpt. The excerpt read does not say who the villagers were, and the atlas has not checked. Zelenin’s own conclusions about two classes of the dead have been revised since, and the plate takes from him only what local people were reported to do and to fear.

sections.heading: The ravine at Orkino
paras: The second report in Zelenin concerns Orkino, in Saratov uezd. There sudden deaths, drunkards, the drowned and suicides were buried far from the village, in the forest, in a ravine between two steep hills.

The Orkino report concerns half-Russified Mordvins, not Russians. It is on this plate openly, as a neighbouring tradition in the same governorate that shows the same placing of the dead, and it is not counted as evidence for Russian custom. It was read through an excerpt, and no page number is available.

sections.kicker: PART III · ESTONIAN AND BELARUSIAN ARCHIVES
sections.heading: The forest on the road
paras: A 2025 comparative study of forest spirits by Mare Kõiva, Elena Boganeva and Ilya Butov remarks that in many rural cultures the forest is a place of hostile forces, or even of hell, and that the road to the realm of the dead is thought to run through it. The authors take that remark from an earlier author, Ivanov (1992), and present it as a common belief, not as their own finding.

The article’s sources are archives in Estonia and Belarus, with a small Russian-language sample from Estonia. It supports a widespread idea; it does not show how that idea was held in any Russian village.

sections.heading: A hut at the treeline
paras: Enrique Santos Marinas, reading the folktales Afanasyev published between 1855 and 1863, argues that the hut of Baba-Yaga stands at the forest edge or in a clearing because that position marks it as a threshold between two realms. On his reading the hut is a gateway to the Other World and its owner guards the passage.

This is a reading of narrative. A tale tells us what a teller expected an audience to recognise, which is not the same as what anyone did with a body. The plate keeps the hut as an image and does not use it as a record of belief.

sections.heading: The leshii as one survey records him
paras: Zelenin’s 1927 survey (1991 translation, pp. 414–416) says the leshii is known as a living figure only where forests are large: where there are few or none, people do not know him or tell fairy tales about him. Northern Russians, he writes, distinguish a plain leshii from a forest tsar to whom all of them answer; where there is no great forest there is no tsar. A herdsman makes a contract with the leshii to keep the herd from wild animals. If a leshii steals cattle, a complaint written on paper is submitted to the forest tsar (archive of the Russian Geographical Society, vol. I, no. 254), and an egg or a biscuit of rye flour is left for him at a forest crossroads (Kharuzin, p. 316). Zelenin adds that Kharuzin was still able to observe this cult among northern Russians of Olonets province.

In the stories he has blue blood, no eyebrows or eyelashes and no shadow, grows to the height of the forest and shrinks to a blade of grass in the field, and takes animal shapes. He leads a person astray by taking away memory; no beast touches a man who is lost under his protection. He may tickle a woman to death or carry her off and have children by her. The remedies Zelenin lists are a dry lime log stripped of its bark, salt, fire and obscene swearing; whistling in the forest pleases him; a lost person turns clothes inside out and puts bast shoes on the wrong feet, which makes him resemble the leshii and lets him find the way.

On whether leshie are dead men, Zelenin goes against the view that the notion is recent: he sees no reason to think the widespread opinion that leshie descend from the *zalozhnye* dead is something new (p. 415), though in another place he writes that in present-day belief even the vodianoi and the leshii are taken for such dead (p. 410). He is a single compiler of the 1920s. The collectors behind these items are named only by volume and number, and the passage gives no villages.

sections.heading: What this plate does not say
items: It does not say that Russians generally buried anyone in forests. The one other burial report is a single volost in Simbirsk province; it is a report of belief about where a particular kind of dead person belonged, and the excerpt read does not name the villagers.

It does not equate the forest spirit with the dead. Only one source used here links them: Zelenin (1927) reports the opinion that leshie descend from the ‘pledged’ dead, and he sees no reason to think it recent, while saying elsewhere that it belongs to present-day belief. The plate reports that opinion from one compiler and does not decide it; the 2025 articles make no such link.
The Orkino report is Mordvin. Putting it on a plate about Russian death is a choice the plate makes openly and does not hide.

items: Zelenin’s text itself, with page references for each local report and the correspondent named where he names one.
Regional ethnographic collections that record where drowned, suicides and unbaptised children were buried, village by village.
Archaeological or cemetery records of burials outside churchyards, kept apart from folklore.

sections.alt: A black-and-white photograph of two weathered wooden crosses on a low overgrown mound under a birch, a wide river behind, and worn curved timbers lying in the grass in the foreground
sections.caption: Old graves in the forest of Kureika, Yenisei region, 8 September 1913. Photographed by Fridtjof Nansen on his Siberian journey: two long-abandoned graves with wooden crosses under birches at the edge of a river bluff, worn timbers in the foreground that Nansen reads as the remains of an old sledge. He tentatively took the dead person for a Yenisei Ostyak and read the sledge as laid on the grave so the dead could ride to the other world. Historical note: this is Nansen’s observation and interpretation of one burial site, not evidence of a general Ket or Russian funerary practice.

plates.title: WATER, MARSH AND RIVER
plates.subtitle: Where the drowned were remembered, and where the swamp stood between worlds
plates.dek: In the sources read for this plate, water is the place of the drowned, the swamp is a border, and the water’s owner keeps those who drown. A calendar day remembered those who died by water; an essay reads swamps as a threshold; two older writers report what was said of the water spirit. A lament and a song are printed beside them as texts, not as records of a rite. The plate keeps the dated custom and the interpretation apart.
plates.marginal: The calendar custom is reported by regions. The swamp essay spans many peoples and is not a Russian survey. The water-spirit passages come from compilers who name no villages. The two texts are one performer’s lament and a literary song. None of them proves another.
plates.period: Customs recorded 19th–20th centuries; handbooks 1903 and 1927; essay 2022; lament recorded 1867–1868; song 1883
plates.location: Vyatka, Smolensk and other provinces (Semik reports); Russia and neighbouring peoples (essay)
plates.tradition: Eastern Slavic folk custom; comparative mythology

sections.heading: A landscape in between
paras: Olga Lavrenova’s essay reads swamps in the mythopoetic picture of the peoples of Russia as a border landscape. A swamp joins water and land without being either, and in many of her examples it is also a place where souls go and where the living are in danger. Swamp spirits drag people down or lure them into the mire, and the kikimora of some accounts is a girl who drowned in a swamp.

The essay is a humanities argument built on secondary collections and has no stated way of choosing its examples. It ranges across Slavic, Finno-Ugric, Tungus, Turkic and other peoples, so a single detail cannot be assumed to be Russian. It tells us what a swamp can mean in these traditions. It does not tell us what any family did when someone drowned.

sections.alt: A wet bog with low pines and pools of standing water under a cloudy sky
sections.caption: A bog by Lake Lelikozero, Medvezhyegorsk district, Karelia, August 2014. Photograph: Evgenii Ievlev, CC BY-SA 4.0. A present-day landscape in the Russian North, shown to give the word ‘swamp’ a place. It is not tied to any rite.
sections.credit: Evgenii Ievlev / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

sections.heading: The drowned at Semik
paras: The Great Russian Encyclopedia’s online entry on Semik, the Thursday of the seventh week after Easter, describes it as a time to remember people who died without repentance or a funeral: the drowned, the hanged, victims of violence and the unidentified. It also says that in Vyatka the day was given to the drowned and that cemetery feasts there turned boisterous; the Zelenin passages read for this plate do not confirm that, and tie Vyatka to poor-house sites instead (below). In Smolensk province people avoided washing, rinsing or any work with water on that day so that no one in the family would drown. Wreaths and birches were thrown into rivers, and in some readings whether a wreath floated or sank signalled marriage or death.

Zelenin gives Smolensk province an older record. Peasants there, he writes, remembered the drowned, the hanged and others who had died suddenly on Semik, and he cites Dobrovolsky (1908, p. 14). A second report he cites, by Georgievsky (1894, p. 3), describes a memorial service at the Petropavlovsk parish cemetery in the city of Smolensk for those who died violent deaths and remained unidentified. The ban on water work is not in the part of Zelenin read here; for that the plate has only the encyclopedia.
The entry is anonymous and undated, and it names its regions without quoting the original records. The plate takes them as reports to be checked, not as a finished survey.

sections.heading: Pits for the unclaimed
paras: The same entry says that unidentified and unclaimed bodies were once placed in open communal pits, skudelnitsy, and buried together at Semik. Commemoration took place at cemeteries and at the sites of these ‘poor houses’. It adds that Catherine II banned burial in them in 1771.

Zelenin’s Vyatka material is about these places. He cites Veshchomov (written in 1807, published 1908, p. 192) for memorial services on the Semik Thursday at the former poor-house burial ground in Khlynov, the city of Vyatka, where executed criminals and unclaimed poor had been buried. Glushkov (1862, pp. 27–30) describes a festive commemoration at Kotelnich, with egg-throwing and clay-ball fights. Zelenin’s own record of 1904 (p. 161) puts the commemoration at Ledovo, Yaransk district, on the Saturday after Trinity, at the site of a former poor house. These are reports in a compilation, each tied to a named place and, in the original, to a named collector; the originals were not seen here.

That is a record of an institution, a place and a date. It is useful here because it shows the calendar custom attached to a physical arrangement for the dead who had no family to bury them. It says nothing about rivers.

sections.heading: The water’s owner and what he did with the drowned
paras: In his handbook of East Slavic ethnography, Dmitry Zelenin devotes § 159 to the *vodyanoi*. He writes that fishermen and millers knew him best, and sometimes offered him sacrifices; that he helped a fisherman and guarded a miller’s dam, but when angry tore nets, drove off fish and flooded hives; and that a person who bathed at noon or at night could be pulled into his kingdom. Rescuing a drowning person was dangerous, since the *vodyanoi* might drown the rescuer, now or later, for taking his victim. The drowned became his workers, and girls became rusalki and often his wives. By the idea common to all East Slavs, he adds, the *vodyanoi* were themselves once ‘pledged’ dead, that is drowned people (1991 edition, p. 416).

Maksimov’s 1903 book gives the same fear in practical form: bruises and scratches on a body taken from the water showed that the person had been in the spirit’s paws, and a wooden cup with three wax candles fixed to its rim, set on the water, would sink and stop over the place where the drowned lay (pp. 77–78, 83–84). Both writers are summarising many local reports, and neither names a village for these items, so they show a belief that scholars of the time considered widespread in northern and central Russia, and not its distribution. The one firm point where they overlap with the Semik material above is that the drowned were a category apart: dead by water, outside the churchyard’s ordinary care.

sections.heading: Water, source by source
rows: That some places remembered the drowned on a set day and avoided water on it
That swamps can be read as a border and a route for the dead in these traditions
Zelenin, 1916 (chapter 4 on Semik, read in the 1995 reprint)

That Semik commemoration of the drowned and the unidentified is recorded for Smolensk and, at poor-house sites, for Vyatka; and that the dead of ‘unnatural’ death were given a place in waters, bogs and thickets

That the water’s owner is described as taking those who bathe at the wrong time, keeping the drowned as workers, and that the opinion is reported that he was himself a drowned ‘pledged’ person; not the distribution of any belief
A collector’s book; no place or informant for these items
That bruises on a drowned body were read as the spirit’s grip and that a floating cup with candles was said to find the body; not where, or how widely

sections.heading: What this plate does not say
items: It does not say that all Russians feared swimming or buried the drowned in a particular way. The sources used give isolated regional customs.

The Zelenin chapter on Semik was read through a summary of an online copy, and the authorities he cites were not seen. The statement about the afterlife in waters and thickets is general and not tied here to a village. Maksimov was read by keyword search, not in full.

The water spirit, rusalki and swamp spirits are not treated here as the drowned themselves. Some sources do report that link as an opinion: Zelenin (1927) gives the East Slavic view that the vodyanoi were once drowned ‘pledged’ dead and that drowned girls became rusalki, and Lavrenova cites kikimoras described as girls drowned in a swamp. The plate passes these on as the sources’ statements and does not decide them; that question belongs to plate T, *The Unquiet Dead*.

The lament and the song printed below are texts. The lament is one performer’s, in one province; the song is a literary poem of 1883 that became a folk song. Neither is evidence for a rite, and the song’s ‘princess’ is a literary figure.

sections.heading: What would turn this plate into a study
items: The original records behind the Semik entry and behind Zelenin’s citations (Dobrovolsky 1908, Georgievsky 1894, Veshchomov, Glushkov, Zelenin 1904), with collector, place and year.
Parish burial registers and police records for drownings, where archives allow it.
Studies of river and lake rites in the Russian North, read in full.
The full text of Zelenin’s chapters on water, with page references.

plates.title: ROADS, CROSSROADS AND BORDERS
plates.subtitle: Parting at the last crossroads, a reconstructed rite, and the crosses beside a modern highway
plates.dek: A crossroads is where a village ends, where relatives are seen off, and, in one scholar’s reconstruction, where some of the dead were once buried. A modern field count of roadside memorials gives the plate something firmer: 299 signs on three highways. The plate keeps the old reconstruction and the new count apart.
plates.marginal: The crossroads rite is a hypothesis built on fragments. The 299 signs are counted and photographed, but they mark road deaths of 1965–2019 in three Volga republics.
plates.location: Russian North (reconstruction); Chuvashia, Tatarstan and Mordovia (count)
plates.tradition: Eastern Slavic folk custom; contemporary roadside commemoration

sections.heading: Parting at the last crossroads
paras: N. A. Krinichnaya’s 1997 article on the crossroads, the Russian rosstan, records that it was the usual place to see travellers off and to wait for relatives returning after a long absence. The custom of parting at the village edge, at the nearest crossroads, she says, survived into her own time. Her material is mainly from the Russian North: Karelia, the Onega region, Vologda and Kostroma.
The article’s subject is fate, and parting is a side topic that it handles briefly. It gives no figures for how common the custom was.

sections.alt: A tall wooden Orthodox cross beside a snowy road junction, with a pine wood behind and a blue sign reading Reshma
sections.caption: A wooden cross at the turn to Reshma, Ivanovo Oblast, November 2011. Photograph: A-DIR, CC BY 3.0. The file does not say what the cross commemorates, and the plate does not guess.
sections.credit: A-DIR / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0

sections.heading: A crossing as a burial ground
paras: Krinichnaya traces burial at crossroads to ancestor cults. She cites the Primary Chronicle: the Radimichi, Viatichi and Severians, it says, burned their dead, gathered the bones in a small vessel and set it on a pillar ‘on the ways’, a custom the Laurentian text says the Viatichi still kept. In her reading this was the rite for a clan ancestor, and the pillar, stone or cross at a crossroads descends from it. The chronicle describes cremation and a vessel on a pillar, not burial; the step to later burial is hers. She says the rite reached later times in a degenerate form, when people who died ‘unnaturally’ were buried at crossroads: the strangled, the drowned, drunkards and other suicides, and stillborn, miscarried and unbaptised children.

This is a reconstruction. It rests on fragmentary and often nineteenth-century records and on the idea of survivals, and the author’s own framing makes much of it hypothetical. The plate offers it as one scholar’s argument. It does not establish that any particular dead person was buried at any particular crossing.

sections.alt: A mounted warrior in mail stands before a tall inscribed stone on an open plain at dusk, with bones, a skull and ravens in the grass
sections.caption: *Knight at the Crossroads*, oil painting by Viktor Vasnetsov, 1878. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. The crossroads as an epic image: a stone with a warning, bones in the grass. It shows how the place was imagined in a painted bylina, not what was buried at any real crossing.
sections.credit: Viktor Vasnetsov / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

sections.heading: The roadside today
paras: M. G. Matlin’s geographical study is a continuous survey: he drove sections of three federal highways in the Middle Volga (362 km in all), photographed every roadside memorial sign, recorded its location and asked road workers and residents about it. The visits fall between July 2013 and April 2021, with repeat passes to follow change; the dates on the 299 signs run from 1965 to 2019.

He sorts them into two families. One imitates the cemetery with crosses, steles, obelisks, fenced plots and wreaths. The other does not, and uses flowerpots, gazebos, decorated trees and car parts. The boundary between them is loose. Placement differs by region: in Mordovia most signs stand on slopes, in Tatarstan in the roadside strip and in Chuvashia in or near woodland. He argues this differs from the European and North American habit of placing memorials right at the road edge.

Two limits on the count are the author’s own. Temporary items (live or artificial flowers, wreaths, ribbons, toys) were separated from permanent ones (wood, metal, stone), but the lifespan of the temporary ones could not be established: ten were seen to last one to three years. And the text read does not publish coordinates sign by sign, so this plate does not map them. A second paper by Matlin, read in abstract only, reports that signs giving no information about the dead are 19% of those on R 241, 33% on A 151 and 50% on R 178.

sections.heading: Signs counted on three highways
What this plate does not say
items: It does not say that today’s roadside crosses descend from the crossroads rite. Neither source argues the link.

The count is of road-death signs on three routes in three republics. The author notes that the findings may not hold elsewhere, that density overstates what a driver sees, and that the idea of the road as a cemetery rests on drivers’ comments.
It does not describe the many other roadside cross traditions of Russia and its neighbours. The sources used here do not cover them.

sections.heading: What would turn this plate into a study
items: Regional ethnographic records of crossroads burial, with the place, year and collector named.
Studies of wayside and votive crosses at settlement edges, separate from road-death memorials.
A comparable count of roadside memorials in a Russian-majority region, to test whether the Middle Volga pattern holds.

plates.title: THE VANISHED VILLAGE
plates.subtitle: Flooded towns, uncounted graves and the villages that simply empty
plates.dek: Villages leave the map in two ways: the state floods them, or people leave. The Rybinsk Reservoir covered a town and hundreds of villages; the census records thousands of villages with no residents at all. The plate puts the two side by side and says what is and is not documented about the cemeteries in the flood zone.
plates.marginal: Figures for the flooded area come from a planning proposal. The claim about cemeteries under the water comes from a news feature seen only in an excerpt. Both are marked as such.
plates.location: Rybinsk Reservoir (Yaroslavl, Vologda and Tver oblasts); Russian Federation (census)
plates.tradition: Soviet infrastructure and rural depopulation

sections.heading: Water over the village
paras: E. A. Filatova’s 2026 planning article gives context figures for the Rybinsk and Uglich reservoirs on the Upper Volga: more than 300,000 hectares of fields, meadows and forest flooded, more than forty churches, three monasteries, about seven hundred villages and hamlets, and six towns, among them Mologa and Korcheva.
The article proposes lowering the reservoir to restore settlements, so it argues a case. In the part read, the figures carry no primary citation and there are no figures for graves or cemeteries.

sections.alt: A broad market square seen from above, with horse carts, trading rows, a two-storey stone building and a church with a bell tower in the distance
sections.caption: The market square of Mologa, early twentieth century. Photographer unknown; public domain as given on Commons. It shows the town before the reservoir. It does not show the flooding or the cemeteries.
sections.credit: Unknown photographer / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

sections.heading: Resettlement by decree
paras: I. Tsipileva’s article, written on Cherepovets district, states that resettlement followed a decree of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee and the Council of People’s Commissars of 1 August 1936, and that the residents of about seven hundred villages and hamlets were moved from the flood zone.
Only the opening of the article was seen, and its year of first publication is not shown. The decree is a dated document that a reader can look for. The article’s own focus is one district.

sections.alt: A small wooden chapel topped with a cross and a white bell-towered church on a bare rise, with a few figures between them
sections.caption: Mologa: a chapel and the Church of the Ascension, between 1901 and 1910 by Commons’ estimate. Photographer unknown; public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (the file credits the Runivers project). A view of what was above ground before the water. It does not show the cemeteries, and it says nothing about what was done with them.
sections.credit: Unknown photographer / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

sections.caption: The belltower of St Nicholas Cathedral in Kalyazin, Tver Oblast, standing in the water of the Uglich Reservoir, 7 September 2012. Photograph: Vladimir Pakhomov, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. It is a different reservoir and a different town from Mologa and the Rybinsk Reservoir; it is shown as a sight a flooding leaves behind, not as evidence about Mologa.

Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2021, via Sentinel Hub Playground and Wikimedia Commons. The Commons file only says ‘Place of Mologa city as seen from space’; the atlas does not interpret the shapes.

sections.heading: The cemeteries under the water
paras: A news feature published by RAPSI on 13 July 2026 says that the sanitary preparation of the reservoir bed was meant to include moving cemeteries, that in practice only some churchyards were moved in the 1930s and 1940s, and that many cemeteries of the Mologa area went under the water with their villages. It adds that estimates of the number resettled run from 100,000 to 130,000 and that historians dispute how they were counted.

This is unverified. The page could not be fetched, the lines were read in a search excerpt, and the excerpt cites no records. The plate treats it as a lead: the transfer of burials in the flood zone should be in archival files, and it is not in the sources read for this plate.

A second, personal strand: in a resettled woman's recollection, R. P. Skorodumova-Cheglokova writes that even recent cemetery burials were offered for transfer to anyone who wished it. It is one memory, read in a search excerpt only. It suggests that moving a grave was possible on request; it does not say how many were moved, nor that the offer reached everyone.

sections.heading: Why the flooded villages were remembered late
paras: Galina Yankovskaya, a historian, wrote in 2021 on how the negative effects of Soviet and Russian hydropower projects are being commemorated: flooded land, mass resettlement and the loss of historical and cultural heritage. She says that since the early 2000s a new memorial culture has formed in several regions, with personal activism, memorial signs on flooded territories and church sites, support from state bodies, charities and religious organisations, tourism around the flooded places, contemporary artists, and internet platforms where amateur historians, witnesses and their descendants take part.

Her explanation for the long silence rests on a few causes. For the generation that lived through the Rybinsk reservoir, the war pushed resettlement into the background; the scale of the projects produced a feeling of the ‘electric sublime’ and pride in the new seas, and some children recall joy at the sea they had waited for; builders who arrived from elsewhere had no tie to the drowned old places; and many archive files on the reservoirs were closed until the 2010s. These are her inferences from memoirs and public sources, and the article is about the way the past is now recalled, not about how many villages or graves were lost; it was read here for its abstract, conclusion and the passages around them, not for every case it names.

sections.kicker: Q / A COUNT AND A DAY OF MEMORY
sections.heading: 663 settlements, and a prayer at the water’s edge: a 2009 magazine report
paras: Ivan Yakubov’s 2009 piece in the business magazine *Priamye investitsii* is journalism, not research, and cites no archive for its figures. It says that the Rybinsk reservoir began to fill in April 1941 and went on filling until 1947, and that before the flooding 130,000 people were moved from 663 settlements and the town of Mologa. It adds that the towns of Myshkin, Vesyegonsk, Uglich and Kalyazin were partly flooded and that several monasteries, among them Leushino, were lost with ‘hundreds of churches, villages, cemeteries’, but it gives no number for graves. On the terms of the move it says that owners of houses worn more than 60% had ten days to a month to leave with a small compensation and a loan, while sounder houses were taken down and moved; the quoted citizens’ complaints are about timbers lying on the shore and houses put up without foundations (p. 108).

The 663 settlements differ from the ‘about seven hundred’ of the other sources on this plate, and the plate does not choose between them: the counts come from different unreferenced reports. The second half of the piece is about commemoration. It says that in 1999 pilgrims from the Leushino metochion in St Petersburg set up a wooden cross at Myaksa, the village nearest the flooded convent, and that prayer ‘standings’ have been held there and at other shores since, at the festival of the convent on 7 July; and that 14 April is observed as the day of memory of Mologa (p. 108). These are the organisers’ and the writer’s statements, read once, and show a practice of the 2000s, not an older one.

sections.heading: Two ways a village disappears
rows: Planning article; no primary citation seen
Report of the census report; 48% more than at the previous census

sections.heading: What this plate does not say
items: It does not give a number of graves or cemeteries lost. No source read here does, and the one claim about cemeteries is unverified.

It does not equate a flooded village with an uninhabited one. A flooded village was removed by decision; an uninhabited village in the census is a statistical status that says nothing about surviving buildings.
It does not retell the legends that grew around Mologa. They are not drawn from sources read here.

sections.heading: What would turn this plate into a study
items: Archival files on the transfer of burials from the flood zone, with the decree of 1 August 1936 and the orders that followed.
Parish records and cemetery registers for the flooded parishes, where they survive.
Oral-history collections from resettled families, with consent and attribution settled for private testimony.
The Rosstat census tables, to separate uninhabited villages by cause.

plates.title: THE UNDERGROUND
plates.subtitle: A monastery cut into a ravine, a physics survey, and a tunnel nobody has shown
plates.dek: The plate starts from one documented place: the burial caves of the Pskov-Caves Monastery. It sets what the sources record beside a 2023 muon survey and a legend of a tunnel to Izborsk, and marks which is which. Other underground places stay leads.
plates.marginal: One monastery. One reported figure with no register behind it. One legend, marked as one.
plates.period: Caves in use since the fifteenth century; survey 2023
plates.tradition: Orthodox monastic burial

sections.heading: A cemetery cut into a ravine
paras: The Pskov-Caves Monastery at Pechory, near the Estonian border, is built over a system of burial caves. A pilgrim reference describes the near caves as the monastery cemetery, used at first only to bury monks. A 2023 newspaper account counts seven accessible underground ‘streets’ with a combined length of more than 200 metres.

The figure repeated everywhere is about ten thousand burials. The pilgrim reference gives it as a total and the newspaper as a report; neither names a register. The plate carries the number as a reported size, not as a count.

sections.caption: The courtyard of the Pskov-Caves Monastery in front of the cave church, Pechory, 2015. Photograph: Lobusov D., CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. It shows the buildings above ground. The caves and the burials in them are not visible, and the atlas does not show them.

sections.heading: Looking behind the walls
paras: In 2023 a team of physicists, led according to the newspaper by N. G. Polukhina, laid nuclear-emulsion detectors in the caves to record atmospheric muons, which pass through rock and leave tracks where the rock is thinner or hollow. The method is non-destructive. A paper in the *Bulletin of the Lebedev Physics Institute* reports it for two objects in the cave complex.

The newspaper account gives the results as reported by the team: a hidden passage about 12 m long behind a walled crypt, the continuation of Trinity Street into the hill beyond a barrier, and an unidentified cavity of roughly 3 × 6 × 3 m between two streets. These dimensions are the team’s estimates as quoted, not measurements anyone has opened up and checked.

The authors’ open preprint is more careful than the newspaper. Thirteen detectors were used, two in the attic of the Assumption Church to measure background and eleven underground, and they were exposed for 112 days. The first object is a crypt behind a large icon at the cave entrance, about 2.5 × 2.5 m, with a corridor 1–3 m wide and up to 12 m long running at right angles to Main Street. The second is a cavity near Trinity Street about 2 m high and roughly 3 × 6 m, and the street itself is shown to continue. The preprint gives no formal error margins, calls the sizes rough estimates, and differs from the newspaper on the height of the cavity (about 2 m against 3 m). It gives no number of burials; it says only that the caves were used as a necropolis from the monastery’s founding.
The same account says it is hard to know who dug the spaces, when and why. The question of what lies behind the walls is open, and the plate leaves it open.

sections.heading: The tunnel to Izborsk
paras: Both a 2024 business-newspaper article and the 2023 Rosatom feature repeat the legend that the caves run underground from Pechory to Izborsk. The first puts the distance at about 20 km, the second at about 15 km. The Rosatom feature calls the tunnel legends unverified folklore and attributes them to the monastery’s abbot.
The legend is kept here because it is told, not because it is true. The survey described above looked at two dead ends; it does not bear on a tunnel of that length.

plates.title: HOUSEHOLD SPIRITS
plates.subtitle: The domovoy, the dead and the limits of the ancestor reading
plates.dek: A spirit of the house who is sometimes read as a dead ancestor. The plate sets regional studies side by side (Perm, Arkhangelsk, Kargopol and a multi-region survey), says what each can and cannot carry, and keeps the bannik and the kikimora out of the ancestor story.
plates.marginal: One scholarly reading, two studies, one village, and a survey of students that did not find the belief. The reading is marked contested.
plates.location: Russia: Perm Krai and the regions of the 1999–2015 field collections
plates.tradition: Russian household belief

sections.heading: A householder who may have been a relative
paras: Ethnographic work on Russian belief describes the domovoy as the spirit of a house and its people. O. K. Ansimova and O. V. Golubkova, drawing on an earlier study by N. A. Krinichnaya, call him a generic ancestor: the soul of an ancestor that became the soul of the house and the family. Some of their rural informants still held that view.

The link to the dead runs through events. The same article says the domovoy may be the restless soul of a dead relative, that before a death he may knock or rattle dishes, and that after one he may disturb the house for a period such as forty days. In villages, food was set out for him at commemorations of dead parents.

sections.heading: One village, 2019
paras: M. A. Granova recorded beliefs about the domovoy in Severny Kommunar, in the Sivinsky district of Perm Krai, in June 2019 and compared them with older university-archive material from other districts. Speakers call him domovoy or dedushka-domovoy, ‘grandfather’. She reads such names as possibly pointing to a family ancestor or a dead elder who became the spirit of the house, and the diminutives as a way of appeasing him without naming him.

He is described as a small hairy old man or as an animal, most often a cat or a weasel, and some say only children under five, cats and dogs can see him. Sweets are left for him; tables are not left empty overnight; a fixed formula is spoken to take him to a new house. Some speakers also describe a second, harmful female spirit in the cellar, which Granova says is not recorded elsewhere in the Perm archives she used.

She finds the beliefs much reduced: the spirit has become a figure for frightening children or is merged with the unclean force in general, and the name Kuzka probably comes from a cartoon. She gives this as a tendency. The number of informants is not stated, and the study rests on one village.

sections.heading: Two northern accounts that disagree
paras: For Arkhangelsk Oblast, N. Drannikova writes that the domovoy is usually considered a deceased member of the family and the first ancestor of the clan; in one formulation he is a man who died unrepentant, and he may look like a dead grandfather. She lists about twenty-three names for him and reports that a groan or a knock from him often foreshadows a death in the family. Her field material comes from expeditions of 1990–2012 and earlier collections, and no count of records is given.

For the Kargopol area of the same oblast, K. Denisevich, a student, describes a helpful ‘master’ of the household who looks like the head of the family and cares for horses and cows. Her text does not say that he is a dead person. It says only, in a general statement, that he is closely tied to the ancestor cult. In the same account the baennik of the bathhouse, the ovinnik of the threshing barn and the dvorovoy of the yard are separate spirits, none of them linked here to the dead.

The two accounts are from one oblast and give different degrees of the ancestor link. This is the plate’s reason for keeping the link as a regional report, source by source, and not as a trait of the domovoy.

sections.heading: Under the stove: Zelenin’s inventory of the domovoi
paras: Zelenin’s 1927 survey (Russian translation 1991, pp. 412–414) gives the domovoi an address. Most often he lives under the stove; northern Russians put him in the underfloor, in the corner where the stove stands, but also behind the stove, on top of it, or under the stove pillar, and less often under the door-sill, at a corner of the house, or in the attic by the chimney. The yard and outbuildings belong to a separate spirit, the *dvorovoi* or *khlevnik*, whom Zelenin asks not to be confused with the domovoi, and a further northern spirit lives in the stove itself (*susui*, *sysoi*). When the householder goes away the stove is closed with the oven fork or its damper so that the domovoi does not leave with him (citing Zavoiko, p. 105); on moving house he is carried over on a broom or on the peel used to put loaves into the oven (archive of the Russian Geographical Society, vol. II, no. 749).

He is invisible, but sometimes shows himself in the likeness of the householder, living or dead, or as an old man with long grey tangled hair, sometimes without eyebrows. Northern tales make him a small hairy man who once froze (vol. I, no. 224). Naked, he foretells poverty. There are female domovye (*domania*, *domakha*, *marukha*), and animal forms: most often a cat, dog, cow or calf, rarely a snake, rat or frog. Zelenin gives a northern story of a house in which a snake was killed, after which the floor was covered with sour cream and three members of the family died (vol. II, no. 867). He gives no village for it.

On origin Zelenin cites two legends, both in his view of Christian date: angels driven out of heaven fell where they fell, on a house to become a domovoi, in the forest a leshii, in water a vodianoi (vol. II, no. 784); or the domovoi is a man who died unrepentant, a *zalozhnyi* dead. His own reading is that the domovoi unites the cult of ancestors with that of the hearth fire, the ancestors stronger (p. 412). He derives the oldest name, *mara*, a nightmare spirit, and with it the names kikimora and marukha for the malicious domovoi (p. 413). That sets him against the article cited above, which traces the kikimora to unbaptised infants: two scholarly derivations, neither of them an informant’s explanation.

As to behaviour, Zelenin says the domovoi is in general not malicious but takes revenge when angered: pressing on a sleeper, warm for good and cold for illness; groaning and weeping when trouble threatens the house; plaiting the master’s beard; knocking, pinching, smashing crockery, especially when new owners settle in beside the old domovoi (pp. 413–414). Most of this is told of East Slavs or ‘northern Russians’ together, and the passage does not date it.

sections.heading: Not every spirit of the house is an ancestor
paras: The same article that calls the domovoy an ancestor sorts other household spirits differently. It places the bannik and his female counterpart, the obderikha, in a separate group as the most dangerous and malicious, and it traces the kikimora not to ancestors but to unbaptised dead infants.

So the plate does not offer one class of ‘house spirit’. Even for the domovoy the ancestor reading is one scholar’s argument, repeated by others and kept by some informants; the 2015 urban survey did not find it, and Granova offers it as a possibility in the names. The atlas keeps it as a contested reading, not as the explanation.

Svetlana Tolstaya, summarising Slavic demonology, says the same of house-spirits in general: they come from honoured ancestors of the family, while mermaids, water spirits and vampires come from other kinds of dead. She also notes that the Polesie *domovik* differs from the Russian *domovoy*, since it resembles the householder but has marks of a walking dead man or a devil (2024, pp. 11–12). This is one scholar’s synthesis, with Polesie as her main field, so it supports the ancestor reading for the Slavs as a whole but does not date or map it for Russia.

plates.title: THE UNQUIET DEAD
plates.subtitle: Impure dead, a scholar’s term and a dispute over its origin
plates.dek: Who was kept out of the common cemetery, by which source and in which decade, with a scholar’s term set apart from what informants said and a church-history challenge to the pagan-survival reading.
plates.marginal: One borderland, one district, one abstract-only dissent. The vampire of fiction is kept out.
plates.location: Belarusian-Russian borderland: Vitebsk, Pskov and Smolensk regions
plates.tradition: Russian and Belarusian folk belief about ‘impure’ dead

sections.heading: A name made by a scholar
paras: ‘Zalozhnye pokoiniki’ is a scholar’s term. Dmitry Zelenin brought it into use in 1916, taking it from the dialect of Vyatka, where it meant dead who were ‘covered over’ with brushwood, boards or stakes instead of being laid in the earth. He understood it to reflect a belief that the earth does not receive such dead, and he used it for all the ‘impure’ dead.

V. E. Ovseichik, working on the Belarusian-Russian borderland, declines to extend the word to the whole category: it does not occur in Belarusian or other traditions, and burial methods varied. The plate therefore uses ‘unquiet dead’ and ‘impure dead’ for the category and keeps ‘zalozhnye’ for what Zelenin meant by it.

sections.heading: Three categories in one borderland
paras: Ovseichik’s material, from the Vitebsk, Pskov and Smolensk regions, centres on three groups. Unbaptised children were thought unable to enter paradise and to fly at night asking to be baptised; a symbolic baptism or naming after death is widespread. They were kept out of common cemeteries, a ban the author calls strictly enforced in the first half of the twentieth century. Later records mostly call such children angels.

Suicides, in the same material, were thought to go to the devil, not to the ancestors. In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries the body was often not washed, was buried in the clothes it died in, with no funeral meal and no church service, and sometimes marked with an aspen stake. Reported burial places include crossroads, swamps, a ditch by the cemetery, hills and forest. Respondents expected drought and storms if a suicide lay in the common cemetery.

Sorcerers were ‘impure’ whatever the manner of death, because the devil was thought to take the soul. They were buried outside the cemetery or by its fence. Radical measures are reported: exhuming the body, cutting off the head and setting it between the legs, driving an aspen stake through the body. The author cites one modern informant for this.

sections.heading: What Zelenin wrote in 1927 about the anger of the earth
paras: In his 1927 survey Zelenin says that in the twentieth, as in the nineteenth century, only the dead regarded as unclean and dangerous were buried without a grave: mainly people who died violently, above all suicides, and those who died young, before the term set at birth. Northern Russians call them *zalozhnye*, ‘laid down’, from a burial in which the body is not dug in but left on the ground covered with branches (1991, p. 352). He calls this an old and undoubtedly pagan custom, which is his interpretation and is disputed below. He does not trace the word to Vyatka, as the first section of this plate does; the first statement comes from the 1916 account as read through Ovseichik, the second from the 1927 text itself, and the two are not reconciled here.

What he reports as belief is ‘the anger of the earth’. The earth refuses an unclean body, which comes back to the surface however often it is buried; the buried body does not decay, so the dead can leave the grave at night; and the earth shows its anger in spring frosts and drought that ruin the crops. He finds the last idea in the sermons of Bishop Serapion of Vladimir (died 1274) and in Maxim the Greek, who reached Moscow in 1506, and he cites the Abramka chronicle for 1159, in which Metropolitan Konstantin of Kiev ordered his own body thrown to the dogs outside the city, which made a deep impression (pp. 352–353).

The church, he says, demanded graves for all the baptised, and people dug the unclean bodies up and threw them into remote places; he names cases in sources of the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries (Vladimir, Moscow). The compromise was the *ubogii dom*, also called *skudelnitsa*: a pit under a light shed outside the town, where the bodies of suicides, murder victims, plague dead, vagrants and sometimes people of other faiths were laid without coffin or service, covered with matting and not with earth, and buried together at Semik. He says chronicles report temporary pits in plague years from 1215 and that the houses stood in the towns of the Muscovite state from the sixteenth century to the end of the eighteenth. After a decree of 1771, villagers again dug up such graves and threw the bodies into rivers, bogs, ravines and forests; the last trial he knows of was held in 1913 in Saratov province (pp. 353–354). Dates and cases are his; the chronicles and trial records were not seen for this edition.

By his own time, he writes, villages cared less about the method of burial than about the place: people objected to burial in the common cemeteries, which they held clean and sacred, the shared property of the ancestors, who would not want such neighbours. The drunkards among the unclean dead were believed to suck the moisture from the earth around their graves, which people used to explain drought (p. 354).

sections.heading: Ust-Tsilma: the informants’ own list
paras: T. I. Dronova’s 2024 article rests on interviews and observation at funerals among Russian Old Believers without priests in the Ust-Tsilma district of the Komi Republic, on family manuscripts, and on laments held in the archive of the Komi Scientific Centre. It lists whom the community counts as ‘unclean’ dead: those who died unbaptised; suicides (hanged, shot, drowned); women who died in childbirth; stillborn children; sorcerers; missing persons whose bodies were not buried, soldiers excepted; those killed in peacetime; those struck by lightning; those drowned in unclear circumstances; and those who died in the bathhouse (p. 202). The ‘clean’ are those who died old, baptised infants and youths, those who died early but had made confession, and those killed in war, counted as martyrs. The words she records for the unnatural dead are *samoubivets*, *visel’nik*, *zadavlennik*, *utoplennik* and *utopshoi*; *zalozhnyi* does not occur in the text read (p. 201).

The community’s teacher examines each suicide. Church rule forbids commemoration, but he asks whether the man was in health or ‘without mind’; in the second case the dead could be commemorated at common services and a funeral service held some years later, always with the stress that the death was ‘unclean’. Otherwise only the universal services of the parental weeks name them as ‘and those with them’, without their names, though alms may be given (pp. 202–203). The body was not to be touched with bare hands: it was dragged on hooks to a burial place outside the village, usually a low spot, and put in a pit into which went everything used, the rope, work mittens, the hook. People avoided that place. Suicides began to be buried in the cemeteries in the 1970s on the order of the village administration, which angered the Old Believers; many prayer-leaders held the cemeteries defiled, and some saw the ‘last times’ begin. Until recently such dead ‘dropped out’ of the memory of the living, and it was forbidden to speak their names; now families go to the cemetery and cense the graves but do not hold individual commemorations (p. 203).

For an unbaptised child, if the parents’ neglect was the cause, the death counted as the parents’ sin to be confessed. Some held that such souls cannot find rest, others that they are spiritually blind but not sinful and wait in a ‘southern country’ that is not hell. Relatives watched the grave mound for forty days: if the earth stayed still, or rose, it was a sign of the child’s ‘pleasing to God’ state and a six-week requiem could be sung for him as ‘nameless’; if the mound sank, the child had been harmful to people while in the womb and was not commemorated (pp. 203–204). The Old Believers here are book-readers, and an informant answered from a patristic text on those who die suddenly and in water; the teacher’s answer on a man who falls through river ice was that every untimely death must be judged separately. This is one district, one researcher, informants whom she does not name, and a community that reads and weighs written church rules, so its list is an insider’s judgment, not evidence for any wider region (pp. 201–204).

sections.heading: Unbaptised and early dead children: what a Slavic survey allows for Russia
paras: Irina Sedakova’s 2020 article in Folklore 80 surveys the death and funeral of a child across the Slavic world from archive and field data of the late nineteenth to mid-twentieth century. She says that her own records come mainly from Bulgarians in Bulgaria and in diaspora (p. 48). Almost all of what follows is therefore Slavic or Bulgarian, and only a few lines are attributed to Russian places.

Her general statement is that a child who died without baptism and a name was thought to go to hell ‘as if not born’, and that the belief that such children become evil spirits is widespread. She lists the burial places assigned to them (beneath the house, under a window, in the yard, under a tree) without separating the regions in the passage read (p. 56). For baptised children the Russian items are these: in the Russian North a thread as long as the father’s or mother’s height was put in the coffin so that the dead child would not outgrow the parent and ‘walk’ (citing Listova 2001, p. 623); in the Vologda region an egg was put under the pillow of a small child (citing Vlasova 1999, p. 392) (p. 58). Russians, citing Naumenko 1998, p. 116, hold that a child of two or three becomes an angel and one of seven goes to heaven; the fate of an eight-year-old is judged by sins (pp. 61–62).

These are second-hand citations to ethnographic compilations, and the article does not say which village or decade lies behind each. They are enough to show that the fear of the unbaptised dead was Russian as well as southern Slavic. They are not enough for a Russian map of child burial; for that the plate would need the primary regional records.

sections.heading: Two kinds of dead, and the acts that kept the unclean ones out
paras: Svetlana Tolstaya divides the Slavic dead into two groups: the pure, who died a normal death and come back at fixed times without harming anyone, and the unclean (Russian *zalozhnye*), who died early or by violence, such as suicide, hanging or drowning, or who dealt with evil spirits in life. She adds that the dead of either kind might return because they were neglected, or because they worried about small children, and that the unclean visits were the ones guarded against (pp. 10–11). Her detailed protective measures come mostly from Polesie, which is not Russia: needle sewn right to left on the shroud, coffin carried out feet first through a side door or the window, a stone or branches on the grave, poppy seed and sand scattered for the dead to count until cockcrow, and the aspen stake (pp. 9–11).

For the Russian North she gives one item: after the coffin was carried out, the floor was swept and the house washed, always towards the exit (p. 10). In the same passage she says that in different Slavic traditions the benches and tables were turned over and the water was poured out, and that East Slavs left inverted pots or bowls on graves; those lines are general and name no Russian place (p. 10). Her closing section adds a larger claim, that most characters of ‘lower mythology’ are the souls of such dead, a view she traces to Zelenin’s work on the rusalka (pp. 11–12).

That last claim is disputed in the literature this atlas uses. Dynin, read for plate U, argues that the rusalka image is recent and composite and that Zelenin’s origin from the ‘pledged’ dead explains only part of it. The sentence on the plate therefore stays at what Tolstaya says about the dead, and not at what the figures of folk demonology ‘really’ are.

sections.heading: What Maksimov wrote about suicides and the drowned
paras: Sergei Maksimov’s *Nechistaia, nevedomaia i krestnaia sila*, published in 1903 by Prince Tenishev’s Ethnographic Bureau after Maksimov’s death, is a general book on spirits by a writer and collector; it gives few sources for individual items and the editors say they completed the manuscript. It is used here for statements that are short and concrete, not as a survey of practice.

On suicides he writes that pious and strict people judged one who laid hands on himself to be ‘the devil’s ram’ (*chertu baran*), and that the drowned and the hanged were buried, where possible, on the very spot where they had committed the sin, in a bare mound, without a cross and outside the cemetery fence, ‘so that they fall more surely into the power of the unclean’ (pp. 16–17, as marked in the online copy of the 1994 reprint). On water, he says that bruises and scratches on a drowned body showed that the person had been in the *vodyanoi*’s paws, and that to find a body one set a wooden bowl with three wax candles afloat, and it stopped over the place (pp. 77–78, 83–84). On the wandering of such souls he adds that the girls who died by suicide cannot turn back from the state of a rusalka, and that children smothered by their mothers in sleep passed to the ‘secret people’ and were counted lost unless the mother saved them by forty days of prayer and strict fasting (pp. 20–21, 89).

The three items agree with what the plate gets from Zelenin, Dronova and Tolstaya: a burial away from the churchyard for the self-killed and the belief that the water kept its dead. They add no place and no informant, so each is evidence for what an educated collector of the 1890s held to be the common belief, and not for a named village.

Barsov, writing about the Olonets North in 1872, records that miscarried and unbaptised children were buried outside the cemetery fence in a swamp, and sometimes under the floor of the house; that a suicide in Voezersky parish, Kargopol district, was buried five versts from the church, where passers-by usually laid stones or sticks, burning the sticks when many had gathered (a footnote credits this report to L. Malinovsky); and that those who had hanged themselves in Andoma were buried on a hill among fir trees, face down (pp. 312–313). These are two or three places, not a map, and the Church did not prescribe the acts. They match in kind what the plate has from other regions: a site apart, stones or sticks left by passers-by, a turned body.

sections.heading: Walking dead and literary vampires
paras: Ovseichik reports that sorcerers were believed to walk after death, harming people and drinking their blood, and adds that this is rare in the East Slavic area and more typical of South Slavic vampire lore. The borderland material is mostly about where and how the impure dead were buried, not about what they did once they rose.

The upyr’ of nineteenth-century Russian fiction is another matter. One thesis abstract places the literary vampire as a device used in Russian writing from the eighteenth century on, built on older belief. The atlas keeps the two apart: the field records read for this plate do not describe a figure like the literary vampire, and nothing here is evidence for one.

sections.heading: Zelenin and his critics
paras: Zelenin’s 1916 compilation gathered reports from many provinces under one heading and read them together as a single belief: that the earth does not accept the dead of ‘unnatural’ death, who therefore stay among the living. He tied the category to the rusalki. The sources read for this plate raise three objections.

Ovseichik will not extend the word ‘zalozhnye’ beyond its Vyatka use, because it is absent from Belarusian and other traditions and because burial methods varied. Avdeev, from epitaphs and letters of church hierarchs, argues that the related superstitions are of Christian times and not pagan survivals; only his abstract was read. Baiburin’s critique of reading rites as survivals of an earlier religion is a general objection to the method, not a verdict on Zelenin’s evidence.

What remains usable is the dated record. The local reports in the compilation, such as the ravine burials on plate N and the Semik citations on plate O, are evidence of what someone wrote down, from whom and where. The unifying belief is Zelenin’s construction. Where the record is read here, it is cited by place.

sections.heading: A dispute about where the rule came from
paras: Ethnographers of the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries took such burial customs for pagan survivals. A. Avdeev argues the opposite for Muscovite Russia: from sixteenth to early eighteenth-century epitaphs and letters of church hierarchs he finds no obstacle to cemetery burial or regular commemoration of those who died violent deaths, and he holds that the related superstitions arose in Christian times.

This plate has the abstract only. It cannot say how strong Avdeev’s evidence is or how far his conclusion reaches beyond the Muscovite sources. It is placed here so that the pagan-survival reading is not left standing alone.

sections.heading: A rule remembered, 2018–2019
paras: A. Ryko’s fieldwork in the Khislavichi district of the Smolensk region found only remnants of such beliefs. Informants born in the 1930s remember that those who hanged or drowned themselves were not taken to the common cemetery; younger people say they know nothing of it and that the drowned lay in the cemetery. Unbaptised infants were not counted as ‘unclean’ there. No one now says that certain dead can return and harm the living.

Set beside Ovseichik, the two studies cover neighbouring districts and different decades of the same century, and they do not agree on unbaptised children. The author says the findings rest on memory and that it is not clear whether the trend is local.

plates.title: THE CALENDAR OF THE DEAD
plates.subtitle: Church Saturdays, a Thursday the Church lacks and a cemetery day today
plates.dek: A table of who named which day of commemoration, in registers kept apart: the Church, the movable Easter calendar, the Komi-Permyak region and today’s cemetery. The parish is an open gap, and the question of origin is left open.
plates.marginal: One church text, one Komi-Permyak comparison, one 2016–17 field study. The pagan-origin story is not used.
plates.location: Church calendar; Komi-Permyak districts; Kostroma and Vladimir regions
plates.tradition: Orthodox church calendar and regional folk practice

sections.heading: The Church’s own list
paras: In a church instructional text, Hieromonk Job (Gumerov) names the Saturdays on which the Church commemorates the dead: Meat Fare Saturday, the second, third and fourth Saturdays of Great Lent, Trinity Saturday and St. Demetrius Saturday. He explains the choice of Saturday by its place as the day of rest, and says the Lenten Saturdays stand in for the daily memorial services that are suspended during the fast.

He gives St. Demetrius Saturday a precise origin: it was set up after the battle of Kulikovo in 1380, with the blessing of Sergius of Radonezh, first for the soldiers who fell and later for all the departed. This is the Church’s account of itself, written by a churchman; it is evidence for what the Church holds, not for what a village did.

sections.kicker: PART II · WHY THE DAYS MOVE
sections.heading: A day counted from Easter
paras: Easter moves from year to year, and the days of commemoration counted from it move with it. A source that says ‘Radonitsa’ or ‘Semik’ is giving a weekday and a week after Easter, not a date of the month. The Church now places Radonitsa on the Tuesday of Thomas week, the ninth day after Easter; that was 14 May in 2024. A reference work of 1913 describes it as falling mostly on the Monday of that week and in some places on the Tuesday, so the day itself varied by place and period.

Semik is the Thursday of the seventh week after Easter. Counting from Easter Sunday, that is the forty-fifth day, and Trinity Saturday falls three days later; the counting is this plate’s arithmetic, not a statement in the sources. Semik has no place in the Church’s calendar, which is why Maltsev’s Komi-Permyak material and the encyclopedia treat it as a folk day.
Julian and Gregorian reckoning add a second layer: a family’s date for the same day can differ from the date in a modern table. This plate gives no dates for any year.

sections.heading: A day the church calendar does not have
paras: G. I. Maltsev records the commemoration days of the Komi-Permyaks: Radonitsa, Semik, Trinity Saturday, and the Saturdays before Pokrov and St. Demetrius. He writes that Semik, the Thursday of the seventh week after Easter, is absent from the Orthodox calendar, that priests took no part in it in the late nineteenth century and did from the early twentieth. After Zelenin he reports that those dead by unnatural death were commemorated at Semik, and quotes a Kungur saying that they are deaf and blind except on that day.

He also describes a slow move: the Permyaks began to hold this commemoration on the Saturdays of general remembrance, reasoning that prayers would be heard better then. His material is four recordings by one researcher, from a people who are not Russian. The plate uses it only as a regional comparison for a pattern that Russian sources describe.

Read more fully, Maltsev’s article describes a day called dzollun or sharlun, held at the cemetery, where such dead were often buried at the edge. Suicides were also remembered at home, with food set on a water barrel or on the threshold. Families bring pancakes, pies and bread, which may be left on graves or given away. Priests joined in the early twentieth century, and a memorial service is held today in the Kudymkar diocese. The article rests on published sources, on material from the Kungur and Komi Zyuzda districts, and on the author’s own fieldwork in the Yusva, Gayny and Kosa districts between 1995 and 2016.

sections.heading: A cemetery day, 2016–2017
paras: E. G. Chesnokova’s fieldwork in the Kostroma and Vladimir regions found the main cemetery commemoration falling in either the Easter or the Trinity period, and she says this follows regional zones. Within the period one day carries the main rites, and she divides it into a preparation, a meeting of relatives at the cemetery, a walk among the graves, commemoration at the grave, and a continuation at home.

She finds these days both family occasions and social ones, with their importance held or growing, and says collective commemoration repairs ties weakened by distance and broken family traditions. The abstract does not name the day, and the counts of respondents are not given.

sections.heading: What the three sources do not settle
paras: The sources do not say where the folk days came from. A common account makes Radonitsa and Semik pagan spring feasts of the dead that the Church absorbed, but none of the three read here supports or refutes that, and the one popular essay on the subject that came up in searching was not used. What they show is narrower: two calendars that overlap, one the Church’s and one regional, and a regional practice that was moved toward the Church’s Saturdays.
The atlas therefore marks the origin question as contested and leaves it open. The calendar here is a table of who named which day, not a history of how the days arose.

sections.heading: Burying the rusalka at Bolshaya Vereika
paras: In the village of Bolshaya Vereika, Zemlyansk district, Voronezh oblast, women and girls ‘led’ or ‘buried’ a rusalka each year. N. P. Grinkova collected the rite twice, in 1925 and in July 1936, mainly from the storyteller A. K. Baryshnikova, who directed it in performance; she also acquired the figure and its props for the State Museum of Ethnography (collection no. 5866, 1936). The figure was a sheaf of reed (*kuga*), less often of straw, about a metre high, with cross-stalks for arms, a white cloth for a face, and a woman’s embroidered shirt, skirt and headscarf. It lay on a stretcher under a white cloth and three embroidered towels, so that only the head showed, like a dead woman laid out.

The procession set out from the house where the figure was dressed, in holiday clothes, with reed stems for candles. One woman took the part of the priest: hair loose, a mat over her shoulders for a chasuble, and a worn bast shoe swung as a censer. She led a dance-tune song through the village and the others took up the refrain. In the rye field the figure was stripped, the towels and ribbons removed, and figure and stretcher poles thrown into the ditch at the field’s edge. The day was the *zagovenye* after Trinity, the last Sunday before the Apostles’ Fast.

Baryshnikova gave two reasons: thrown into the rye, the rusalka makes the bread grow better; and the rite protects from rusalkas, who would frighten people all summer if it were not done. Women of the older generation took it seriously, and before 1917 the estate steward let women off work for it. The women said it was last done in 1935; in spring 1936 ‘somehow they did not gather’, and in July 1936 Grinkova saw only a staged reconstruction.

The comparisons and the frame are Grinkova’s own: she places the rite among ‘burials of Kostroma’ and the cuckoo, cites Zelenin’s records of rusalka processions in Serdobsk district (Saratov province) and in Ryazan province, and reads all of them as survivals of a dying-and-resurrecting deity cult after Frazer. That interpretation is not adopted here. The record itself is a single village, recorded by one ethnographer from one main informant (pp. 178–181).

sections.heading: The rusalka: a southern name that reached the North late
paras: Vladimir Dynin’s 1994 article in *Etnograficheskoe obozrenie* sets out how the East Slavs described the rusalka, using published provincial reports of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and recent expedition notes. In the south of Russia, in Ukraine and in part of Belarus she is mostly a young, beautiful girl with loose, long hair, and she is usually the soul of a drowned woman or of a child who died unbaptised; these are the places linked to the Trinity–Semik season and the rites of ‘seeing off’ the rusalka. In the Russian North, he says, the same word was not known until recently: correspondents of Tenishev from northern provinces said so, and Zelenin showed that it arrived there in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries with town culture. Northern informants described a shaggy woman with long hanging breasts who combs her hair on a rock or a snag and who is called by other names: *vodyanikha*, *chertovka*, *leshachikha*. One recorded remark from the Kholmogory district runs that ‘now they call them rusalki, and before it was all *chert*’ (pp. 112–113).

His conclusions are that the figure is missing from northern demonology, that it was still unsettled in the south, and that the earliest reports of the rusalka as such date from the eighteenth century. He therefore holds that the image is recent and was built from several beings: *poludnitsy*, wood and water spirits, and the dead honoured in ‘rusalia’ week. He derives the name from *rusalia*, a term he links to the Roman *Rosalia* memorial rite, and he adds that the cult of the ‘pledged’ dead, as Zelenin noted, spread widely in the eighteenth to twentieth centuries (pp. 113–114, 117–118).

This is one side of an open argument. Dynin himself lists others who took the rusalka as an ancient nature spirit, as the dead ancestors, or as a female deity of moisture, and he says that none of these views has been generally accepted (p. 111). The plate therefore uses the article for what it records about regions and names, and treats the late-origin thesis as contested. Pages are taken from the running heads of the supplied PDF.
